ec2.a: Eddie rents you virtual computers, called instances, that you can resize. You pick the processor (CPU), memory, disk and operating system, and pay for compute only while it runs.
ec2.simple: Eddie rents you computers in the cloud. You pick how big they are and pay only while they run.

ec2.a: An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a template holding the operating system and software a server (instance) starts from. Build your own AMI and every new instance boots ready to work, identical each time.
ec2.simple: An image is a recipe for a server: every new server made from it starts up the same, ready to work.

ec2.q: How are Linux On-Demand EC2 instances billed?
ec2.a: By the second while it runs, with a 60-second minimum. Stopping it ends compute charges, but its attached disks (EBS volumes) are still billed for storage.
ec2.simple: You pay by the second while it runs. Stop it and the computer bill stops, but its disks still cost a little.

ec2.q: What does a security group do for an EC2 instance?
ec2.a: It is a stateful virtual firewall at the instance level. You write allow rules only. Return traffic for an allowed connection is let through automatically.
ec2.simple: A security group is a guard at the server's door: it only lets in what you allow, and replies get out.

ec2.q: Why put EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer?
ec2.a: The group replaces unhealthy instances and adds or removes capacity as demand changes. The load balancer spreads traffic across AZs. Together they make the app self-healing and elastic.
ec2.simple: A team of servers that swaps out sick ones and grows or shrinks with the crowd, sharing visitors out fairly.

ec2.q: How much notice do you get before a Spot Instance is interrupted?
ec2.a: A two-minute interruption notice before a stop or terminate. If the interruption behaviour is hibernate, the instance hibernates without that warning. Spot suits stateless, fault-tolerant work, and you should stay flexible across instance types and AZs.
ec2.simple: Spot servers are spare ones on sale, but you get just a two-minute warning before they're taken back.

ec2.q: Why should you require IMDSv2 on instances?
ec2.a: IMDSv2 needs a session token, which you get with a PUT request. That blocks many SSRF-style attacks that try to steal instance role credentials from the metadata service.
ec2.simple: The safer way to ask a server about itself needs a secret ticket first, so tricksters can't steal its keys.

ec2.q: Cluster vs spread vs partition placement groups?
ec2.a: Cluster packs instances close for low-latency networking (HPC). Spread puts each on distinct hardware for isolation. Partition groups racks for big distributed systems like HDFS.
ec2.simple: Placement groups choose where servers sit: huddled close for speed, apart for safety, or in separate racks.

ec2.q: Savings Plans, Reserved Instances or Spot: which saves money when?
ec2.a: Savings Plans: commit to an amount of spend per hour for 1 or 3 years. Reserved Instances: commit to an instance setup, such as type and Region, for 1 or 3 years. Spot: unused capacity at a big discount, for work that can be interrupted.
ec2.simple: Promise steady use for one or three years and pay less. Or use spare servers cheaply, if the job can stop.

ec2.q: What happens to instance store data when you stop an instance?
ec2.a: It's gone. Instance store disks are physically attached to the host and kept through a reboot, but every block is erased when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates. Use them for caches and scratch data; keep anything valuable on EBS, S3 or EFS.
ec2.simple: It's wiped. Built-in disks survive a restart but are erased when the server stops. Keep real data elsewhere.

lambda.a: Like Lola cooking only when an order comes in, Lambda runs your code when an event happens, such as a file upload or a web request. There are no servers to manage, it scales on its own, and you pay per request and for how long the code runs.
lambda.simple: Like Lola cooking only when an order comes in, Lambda runs your code only when something happens.

lambda.q: How long can one Lambda run last (the maximum timeout)?
lambda.a: 15 minutes (900 seconds) per run, called an invocation. For longer multi-step work, use Lambda durable functions (up to a year) or Step Functions workflows, or run it as a container on ECS or Fargate.
lambda.simple: One run can last up to 15 minutes. Longer jobs need a different tool, like Step Functions or a container.

lambda.a: You pay per request plus run time, measured in GB-seconds (memory size × seconds run). Normal on-demand functions cost nothing while idle, but provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed copies) and Lambda Managed Instances are billed even when idle.
lambda.simple: You pay for each run and for how long it cooks. Normally, no orders means no bill.

lambda.q: How does memory setting affect a Lambda function?
lambda.a: Memory ranges from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and CPU is allocated in proportion to memory. More memory can make CPU-bound code finish faster. Test to find the cheapest setting.
lambda.simple: More memory also brings more thinking power, so code can finish faster. Test to find the cheapest size.

lambda.q: What is the default Lambda concurrency quota per Region?
lambda.a: 1,000 concurrent executions per Region by default, shared by all functions. New accounts start lower, and the quota can be raised. Reserved concurrency both guarantees and caps one function's share.
lambda.simple: By default up to 1,000 copies can run at once in a Region, shared by all your functions. You can ask for more.

lambda.q: What is a cold start and how can you reduce it?
lambda.a: The delay while Lambda sets up a new execution environment. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments ready. SnapStart restores from a snapshot, for Java, Python and .NET.
lambda.simple: A cold start is the short wait while a new kitchen is set up. Warm kitchens get reused; some can stay ready.

lambda.q: What are Lambda destinations for asynchronous invocations?
lambda.a: They send a record of each async invocation, on success or failure, to SQS, SNS, EventBridge or another function. S3 is also a target, for failures only. Records carry more detail than a plain DLQ.
lambda.simple: Destinations send a note about each background run, whether it worked or failed, to a place you choose.

lambda.q: Max synchronous invocation payload for Lambda?
lambda.a: 6 MB each for request and response. Streamed responses can reach 200 MB, and async invocations allow 1 MB. Pass large inputs by reference, e.g. an S3 key.
lambda.simple: Each request and each reply can carry up to 6 megabytes. For big files, send where the file lives instead.

lambda.q: What happens when Lambda hits its concurrency limit?
lambda.a: Extra requests are throttled. Synchronous callers get a throttling error (429) and should retry, while Lambda retries asynchronous events for you for up to 6 hours. Reserved concurrency guarantees a key function its share, and provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialised so latency stays steady.
lambda.simple: When every cook is busy, new orders are turned away for a moment. Retry, or save some cooks for key dishes.

lambda.q: What is a Lambda durable function?
lambda.a: A normal Lambda function that saves its progress with checkpoints and replays after a pause or failure. Finished steps are skipped and their stored results reused, so one durable execution can run for up to a year.
lambda.simple: A function that saves its progress, so it can pause for a long time and pick up where it stopped.

lambda.q: In a durable function, what does waitForCallback do?
lambda.a: It suspends the execution until an outside system sends a callback, such as a customer's reply or a manager's approval. The other system answers with SendDurableExecutionCallbackSuccess or Failure, and the function carries on.
lambda.simple: It pauses the function until another system answers, like a customer replying to a text.

lambda.q: Why must code outside steps in a durable function be deterministic?
lambda.a: On replay the handler runs again from the top. Completed steps return their saved results, but code outside a step runs again, so random numbers, timestamps and calls to other systems belong inside steps.
lambda.simple: After a pause the code reruns from the start, so anything random or time-based must sit in a saved step.

lambda.q: Do durable function steps run exactly once?
lambda.a: No. Steps are at-least-once by default: an interrupted attempt runs again on replay. At-most-once per retry waits for the start checkpoint and raises StepInterrupted instead. For at most once overall, also turn retries off.
lambda.simple: No. By default a step may run twice, so make it safe to repeat, or pick at-most-once with no retries.

lambda.q: What are the fixed size limits of one durable execution?
lambda.a: 30,000 durable operations and 100 MB of persisted data per execution, with at most 1 MB per operation payload. These quotas are fixed and can't be raised.
lambda.simple: One run can hold 30,000 saved operations and 100 megabytes of data, and those limits can't be raised.

lambda.a: A way to run Lambda functions on current-generation EC2 instances in your own account. Lambda still handles the instance lifecycle, patching, routing, load balancing and scaling, and EC2 Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply.
lambda.simple: Lambda functions running on EC2 servers in your account, with Lambda still doing all the upkeep.

lambda.q: How is Lambda Managed Instances priced?
lambda.a: You pay the EC2 instance price plus a 15% management fee. EC2 discounts such as Savings Plans apply to the compute only, not to the fee.
lambda.simple: The server's normal price plus 15% for Lambda's care. Server discounts don't shrink the 15%.

lambda.q: How does Lambda Managed Instances scale, and does it have cold starts?
lambda.a: It has no cold starts, because it doesn't scale when an invocation arrives. It scales in the background on CPU use and concurrency, absorbs traffic doubling within 5 minutes, and scales down to a set minimum, never to zero.
lambda.simple: It grows ahead of demand by watching how busy the servers are, so no cold starts, but it never stops fully.

lambda.q: What does Lambda tenant isolation mode guarantee?
lambda.a: With TenancyConfig set to PER_TENANT, which can only be chosen when the function is created, execution environments are never shared between tenants. Every invoke must pass a tenant id, with --tenant-id or the X-Amz-Tenant-Id header.
lambda.simple: Each customer gets its own copies of the function's environment, never shared with another customer.

ecs.a: A container orchestration service: it decides where your containers (packaged apps) run, starts them and restarts any that fail. It works with load balancers, IAM permissions and CloudWatch monitoring.
ecs.simple: Captain Cass decides which ship carries each container, starts them and restarts any that stop.

ecs.a: An app packed with everything it needs, so it runs the same on any machine. Containers share the host's operating system core (its kernel), so they start faster and are lighter than virtual machines (VMs).
ecs.simple: A container is an app packed like a lunchbox with everything it needs, so it runs the same anywhere.

ecs.a: ECS itself is free. You pay for the compute your containers use, on EC2 servers or on Fargate (per virtual CPU, memory and storage), and ECS Managed Instances and ECS Anywhere each add a per-instance fee.
ecs.simple: ECS itself is free. You pay for the computers your containers run on.

ecs.q: Task definition vs service in ECS?
ecs.a: A task definition is a blueprint (image, CPU, memory, ports, roles). A service keeps a desired number of tasks running and replaces failed ones.
ecs.simple: A task definition is the recipe. A service keeps the right number of copies running and replaces broken ones.

ecs.q: Task role vs task execution role?
ecs.a: The execution role lets ECS pull images and write logs. The task role gives your application code its own AWS permissions. Keep both least-privilege.
ecs.simple: One role lets ECS fetch your app and write its logs; the other gives your app its own permissions.

ecs.a: They define where tasks run: Fargate, Fargate Spot, ECS Managed Instances or EC2 Auto Scaling groups. A strategy splits tasks by base and weight (e.g. Fargate + Fargate Spot). AWS recommends them over launch types.
ecs.simple: Capacity providers pick which kind of computers your tasks run on, and how to share tasks between them.

ecs.q: Why use the deployment circuit breaker on an ECS service?
ecs.a: It detects when a rolling deployment keeps failing to reach steady state and can automatically roll back to the last working version, reducing outage time.
ecs.simple: If a new version keeps failing to start, the circuit breaker can roll back to the last one that worked.

ecs.q: What does a blue/green deployment give an ECS service?
ecs.a: The new version runs alongside the old one. Traffic shifts only after the new version is healthy, and rolling back just shifts traffic back. It is safer than an in-place update.
ecs.simple: Blue/green runs the new version beside the old. Visitors move over only once it's healthy, and can move back.

ecs.q: How can an ECS service add and remove tasks on its own?
ecs.a: Service Auto Scaling changes the desired task count for you. It can track a target metric (like a thermostat), step on CloudWatch alarms, follow a schedule, predict from past patterns, or follow an SQS queue's backlog per task.
ecs.simple: Set a target, like 'keep the processor half busy', and ECS adds or removes copies of your app to stay there.

ecs.q: How do you get a shell inside a running ECS container without SSH?
ecs.a: Turn on ECS Exec. It uses Systems Manager Session Manager, so you open no inbound ports and manage no SSH keys, on EC2 or Fargate. CloudTrail records who connected, and each command and its output can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
ecs.simple: ECS Exec lets you type commands inside a running container with no open doors or keys, and it keeps a record.

fargate.a: Fargate runs your containers with no servers for you to manage, which is what "serverless" means. You set the CPU and memory for each task (one running copy of your app), and AWS handles the machines underneath.
fargate.simple: Hand Fern your container and hop off: Fargate runs it without you looking after any servers.

fargate.q: Which container services (orchestrators) can run on Fargate?
fargate.a: Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS. You keep using ECS or EKS as usual, and Fargate supplies the computing power underneath.
fargate.simple: Fargate is the engine under ECS and EKS: you keep using them, and Fargate supplies the computers.

fargate.a: You pay for the virtual CPUs (vCPU), memory and any storage beyond the included 20 GB that you request. Billing is per second, from when your container image starts downloading until the task stops, with a 1-minute minimum on Linux and 5 on Windows.
fargate.simple: You pay per second for the size you ask for (computer power, memory, extra storage), with a short minimum.

fargate.q: Which network mode do Fargate tasks use?
fargate.a: awsvpc: each task gets its own elastic network interface and private IP, so security groups apply per task, not per host.
fargate.simple: Each task gets its own network card and private address, so each one can have its own guard rules.

fargate.q: How do you size a Fargate task?
fargate.a: Pick a supported vCPU and memory combination at the task level. Right-size from CloudWatch metrics, since you pay for what you request, not what you use.
fargate.simple: Pick a size that fits. You pay for what you ask for, not what you use, so watch and trim.

fargate.q: Why run Fargate tasks in private subnets?
fargate.a: Tasks have no public IP, and outbound traffic goes via NAT or VPC endpoints. A load balancer or API front door handles inbound. This shrinks the attack surface.
fargate.simple: Keep tasks in private rooms with no public address. A front door greets visitors, so there are fewer ways in.

fargate.a: An ECS capacity provider that runs interruption-tolerant tasks on spare capacity at a discount. It is not available on EKS. Tasks get a two-minute warning (SIGTERM), so use it for stateless or retryable work.
fargate.simple: Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare computers at a discount, with a two-minute warning before they're taken back.

fargate.q: When might ECS on EC2 beat Fargate on cost?
fargate.a: Large, steady workloads packed densely onto EC2 instances can cost less than per-task Fargate pricing. You manage plain EC2 yourself, or ECS Managed Instances lets AWS manage it. Savings Plans discount all of them.
fargate.simple: For big, steady work packed tightly onto servers, ECS on EC2 can cost less than Fargate.

fargate.q: How much disk does a Fargate task get?
fargate.a: At least 20 GiB of temporary (ephemeral) storage on platform version 1.4.0 or later, and you can raise it to 200 GiB in the task definition. Your container image is stored there too, so subtract its size. It's encrypted, and it's gone when the task stops.
fargate.simple: Each task gets a 20 GiB scratch disk, up to 200 GiB if you ask. It's wiped when the task ends.

fargate.q: Do Fargate tasks share a server with other tasks?
fargate.a: No. Fargate runs each task in its own isolated, hardware-virtualised environment. Tasks don't share an operating system, Linux kernel, network interface, temporary storage, processor (CPU) or memory with other tasks.
fargate.simple: No. Each task runs walled off in its own little machine, so one task can't see another's memory or files.

eks.a: Managed Kubernetes, the popular open-source system for running containers. AWS runs and scales its control plane (the part that decides what runs where) across several Availability Zones (separate groups of data centres).
eks.simple: EKS runs Kubernetes, a popular system for managing containers, and AWS looks after its brain for you.

eks.q: What is a pod in Kubernetes?
eks.a: The smallest thing you can deploy in Kubernetes: one or more containers that share networking and storage. A pod's containers always run together on the same node (a worker machine).
eks.simple: A pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that always stay together, like roommates.

eks.a: Each cluster pays an hourly fee for its control plane, higher on extended support (older Kubernetes versions). You also pay for the EC2 or Fargate compute you use, and EKS Auto Mode adds a per-instance management fee.
eks.simple: Each cluster pays an hourly fee for its brain, plus the computers your containers use.

eks.q: What are EKS managed node groups?
eks.a: EKS provisions and manages the EC2 worker nodes (in Auto Scaling groups) for you, including graceful node updates, so you handle less node lifecycle work.
eks.simple: Managed node groups mean EKS sets up and updates the worker computers for you, so you do less.

eks.q: How do pods get AWS permissions securely on EKS?
eks.a: Use EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) so each workload gets its own scoped IAM role instead of sharing the node's role.
eks.simple: Give each app its own small set of permissions, instead of all apps sharing the whole machine's set.

eks.a: An open-source node autoscaler that launches right-sized EC2 capacity directly for pending pods and consolidates underused nodes to cut cost.
eks.simple: Karpenter adds just-right computers when apps are waiting, and packs things tighter to save money.

eks.q: How must EKS cluster version upgrades be done?
eks.a: One Kubernetes minor version at a time: control plane first, then nodes and add-ons. Check for deprecated APIs before each step.
eks.simple: Upgrade one step at a time: the brain first, then the workers and add-ons. Check for retired features first.

eks.a: An EKS option where AWS also manages the nodes, autoscaling, networking, load balancing and block storage as built-in components, cutting day-2 operations.
eks.simple: Auto Mode lets AWS also run the worker computers, scaling, networking and storage, so you do less every day.

eks.a: Supporting software every cluster needs, such as the VPC CNI networking plugin, kube-proxy and CoreDNS. As EKS add-ons they come validated by AWS with the latest security patches and bug fixes, and EKS installs and updates them for you.
eks.simple: Add-ons are the helper programs every cluster needs, like networking. AWS checks, installs and updates them.

eks.q: How do you give an IAM role access to a Kubernetes cluster on EKS?
eks.a: Create an EKS access entry. It links an IAM identity to Kubernetes permissions, from an AWS-maintained access policy or a Kubernetes group, all through the EKS API. It replaces editing the old aws-auth ConfigMap and can restore access after a mistake.
eks.simple: Add an access entry: it says which AWS role may use the cluster and what it can do there.

beanstalk.a: Give Beanstalk your code and it deploys and runs the web app for you. It sets up the servers (EC2 instances), load balancing, health monitoring and scaling, or an EKS cluster instead in Cluster mode.
beanstalk.simple: Plant your code and Jack grows the whole website around it: servers, traffic sharing, health checks, growth.

beanstalk.a: There is no additional charge for Beanstalk itself. You pay for the underlying resources it creates, such as EC2 instances and load balancers.
beanstalk.simple: Beanstalk itself is free. You pay for the servers and other things it sets up.

beanstalk.a: The ready-made software stack your app runs on in Beanstalk Standard: an operating system, a language runtime (such as Node.js, Python, Java or Docker), a web or app server, and Beanstalk's own components.
beanstalk.simple: A platform is the ready-made soil your app grows in: an operating system, a language and a web server.

beanstalk.q: Application, version and environment in Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: An application holds versions (labelled code bundles). An environment is the running set of resources hosting one version, e.g. staging or prod.
beanstalk.simple: An application keeps labelled versions of your code. An environment is one version running, like test or live.

beanstalk.a: Web server environments serve HTTP traffic. Worker environments pull jobs from an SQS queue to run background tasks without blocking user requests.
beanstalk.simple: Web server environments answer visitors. Worker environments do background jobs from a queue.

beanstalk.q: Why choose an immutable deployment in Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: It launches a full new set of instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group. They replace the old ones only if they pass health checks. A failed deploy therefore leaves the running instances untouched.
beanstalk.simple: Immutable deploys grow a new set of servers and swap only once they're healthy, so a bad deploy harms nothing.

beanstalk.q: How do you do blue/green with Beanstalk?
beanstalk.a: Deploy to a separate environment, test it, then swap environment URLs (CNAME swap). Rollback is a swap back. Keep databases outside the environment.
beanstalk.simple: Build a second copy, test it, then swap the addresses. Undo is just swapping back.

beanstalk.a: In Beanstalk Standard, .ebextensions config files customise resources and settings. On Amazon Linux 2+, .platform hooks run scripts at deployment stages.
beanstalk.simple: Special settings files and hook scripts let you tweak what Beanstalk builds and run steps during a deploy.

beanstalk.q: All at once, rolling, or rolling with an additional batch: how do they differ?
beanstalk.a: All at once is quickest but your app can be briefly unavailable. Rolling updates one batch of instances at a time: no downtime, but less capacity while it runs. Rolling with an additional batch launches extra instances first, so capacity never drops, but takes longer.
beanstalk.simple: Update every server at once (fast, brief outage), a few at a time (no outage), or add spares first.

beanstalk.q: What do Beanstalk managed platform updates do?
beanstalk.a: They upgrade your environment to the newest patch, or patch and minor, version of its platform during a weekly two-hour maintenance window, with no loss of capacity. They never cross platform branches (major versions), because those can break your app.
beanstalk.simple: Beanstalk can patch your servers' software for you each week in a quiet window, without taking your app down.

s3.a: S3 stores files, called objects, in containers called buckets. Each object is found by its name (its key) and carries extra details (metadata), and a bucket can hold a practically unlimited number of objects.
s3.simple: S3 is a giant lake of files. Each file has a name, and a bucket can hold practically any number of them.

s3.q: How durable is S3 designed to be?
s3.a: 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, so losing a stored object is extremely unlikely. S3 keeps copies on multiple devices and, for most storage classes, in at least three Availability Zones (separate data centre groups).
s3.simple: Built so losing a file is extremely unlikely: S3 keeps copies on many devices, usually in different places.

s3.q: What is the largest single object S3 can store?
s3.a: About 50 TB. One normal upload (a PUT request) takes up to 5 GB, so bigger files use multipart upload, which sends the file in parts. AWS recommends multipart from about 100 MB.
s3.simple: One file can be about 50 terabytes. Big files are sent in parts, like a puzzle posted box by box.

s3.q: How do S3 storage classes differ?
s3.a: They trade storage price against access cost and speed: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for infrequent access, Glacier classes for archives. Intelligent-Tiering moves data for you.
s3.simple: Storage classes are shelves: handy ones for files you use a lot, cheaper ones and deep archives for the rest.

s3.q: Why keep S3 Block Public Access turned on?
s3.a: It overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public, preventing accidental leaks. It is enabled by default for new buckets. To serve public content, use CloudFront.
s3.simple: Block Public Access is a lock that stops your files being shared with the whole world by mistake.

s3.q: What do S3 Lifecycle rules do?
s3.a: They transition objects to cheaper classes or expire them after a set age. Rules can cover old noncurrent versions too, cutting cost without manual clean-up.
s3.simple: Lifecycle rules tidy up for you: they move old files to cheaper shelves, or delete them after a while.

s3.a: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs of objects, so a read after a successful write returns the latest data automatically.
s3.simple: Once you save or delete a file, the very next read sees the change. No stale copies.

s3.q: What does S3 replication need, and what is it for?
s3.a: It needs versioning on both source and destination buckets, plus an IAM role. Cross-Region replication supports DR, compliance and lower latency. Same-Region replication helps aggregate logs.
s3.simple: Replication copies files to another bucket by itself, for backups, rules or speed. Versioning must be on.

s3.a: S3 storage built for tabular data, like rows of sales or sensor readings. Tables live in a new bucket type, a table bucket, in the Apache Iceberg format, and you query them with SQL from engines like Amazon Athena.
s3.simple: S3 Tables store data in rows and columns, like a giant spreadsheet you can ask questions about.

s3.q: What upkeep does S3 Tables do for you?
s3.a: S3 keeps compacting small files into fewer, larger ones, manages snapshots and removes files nothing points to. Queries get faster and storage costs drop without clean-up jobs of your own.
s3.simple: S3 Tables tidy themselves: small files get packed together and leftovers cleaned up, so questions run faster.

s3.q: What is Amazon S3 Vectors for?
s3.a: Storing vector embeddings (numbers that capture what text or images mean) in a vector bucket and finding the most similar ones. It suits RAG, semantic search and AI agents, with no servers to set up.
s3.simple: S3 Vectors stores the meaning of words and pictures as numbers, so you can find the most similar ones.

s3.q: How fast are S3 Vectors queries, and when is it a good fit?
s3.a: Under a second for infrequent queries and as low as 100 ms for frequent ones, so it suits workloads that query now and then. For high query rates, export an index snapshot to OpenSearch Serverless.
s3.simple: Good for searching now and then: answers come in under a second. Very busy searching needs a faster service.

ebs.a: Network hard drives, called volumes, that attach to EC2 servers (instances). This is block storage, used like a raw disk. Data survives stops and reboots, and a volume can outlive its instance.
ebs.simple: EBS is a hard drive for your cloud computer, kept in Bex's locker. Files stay safe when it stops or restarts.

ebs.q: Can an EBS volume attach to an instance in another Availability Zone (AZ)?
ebs.a: No. A volume lives in one Availability Zone (one data centre group) and attaches only to instances there. To move it, take a snapshot (a backup copy) and create a new volume from it in the other AZ.
ebs.simple: No. A disk lives in one zone. To move it, take a snapshot and make a new disk from it in the other zone.

ebs.a: You pay for the size you set, per GB per month, even if the disk sits empty. Some volume types also charge for the speed you reserve, IOPS (reads and writes per second) and throughput, and snapshot backups are billed too.
ebs.simple: You pay each month for the size you choose, even if the disk is empty. Extra speed and backups cost extra.

ebs.q: What baseline performance does gp3 include?
ebs.a: 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size. You can provision more IOPS and throughput independently of capacity, and gp3 is usually cheaper than gp2.
ebs.simple: A gp3 disk comes with good speed at any size, and you can buy more speed separately. Usually cheaper than gp2.

ebs.a: Point-in-time backups stored in S3 behind the scenes. They are incremental, so only changed blocks are saved after the first, lowering cost.
ebs.simple: Snapshots are photos of your disk. After the first one, each saves only what changed, so they cost less.

ebs.q: How can you automate EBS snapshot schedules?
ebs.a: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup create, retain and delete snapshots on a policy, so backups happen without scripts.
ebs.simple: Set a schedule once, and AWS takes, keeps and deletes your disk backups for you. No scripts needed.

ebs.a: Uses KMS keys to encrypt data at rest, in transit to the instance, and in snapshots. Turn on encryption by default per Region so new volumes are always encrypted.
ebs.simple: Encryption scrambles your disk's data with a secret key. Turn it on by default so every new disk is locked.

ebs.a: Lets one Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) volume attach to several instances in the same AZ. Apps must use a cluster-aware file system to avoid corruption.
ebs.simple: Multi-Attach plugs one fast disk into several servers in the same zone, but they must take turns carefully.

ebs.q: gp3 or io2 Block Express: when do you need io2?
ebs.a: gp3 suits boot disks, dev/test and most databases, up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s. Pick io2 Block Express for latency under a millisecond, more than 80,000 IOPS (up to 256,000) or 99.999% durability. Only io1/io2 support Multi-Attach.
ebs.simple: Start with gp3, the everyday disk. Pay for io2 only when a big database needs the fastest, most reliable disk.

ebs.q: When would you pick an HDD volume (st1 or sc1)?
ebs.a: For big streaming reads and writes measured in throughput: st1 for big data, data warehouses and log processing, sc1 for rarely read data where the lowest cost matters. Neither can be a boot volume, and both start at 125 GiB.
ebs.simple: Spinning-disk volumes are cheap and good at reading long files, like logs. A server can't start from one.

efs.a: A shared network drive that grows and shrinks on its own, with no servers to manage. Many EC2 instances, containers or Lambda functions can read and write the same files at once, using the standard NFS file-sharing protocol.
efs.simple: EFS is Effie's well: a shared folder that grows by itself, and many computers can use the same files at once.

efs.q: How is EFS different from EBS?
efs.a: EBS is a disk that lives in one Availability Zone and usually attaches to one instance at a time. EFS is a shared file system that many servers and apps can use at once, across Availability Zones.
efs.simple: EBS is one computer's own disk in one zone. EFS is a shared folder that many computers use, across zones.

efs.a: You pay for the storage you actually use, per GB per month, with no size to set in advance. Other charges depend on your throughput mode (how speed is billed) and on access to some storage classes.
efs.simple: You pay only for the space your files take up each month, with nothing to size ahead.

efs.a: Standard, Infrequent Access (IA) and Archive. Lifecycle management moves files that are not accessed to cheaper classes automatically.
efs.simple: Standard, Infrequent Access and Archive. Files nobody opens move to cheaper shelves by themselves.

efs.q: How do clients reach EFS across AZs?
efs.a: Through mount targets created in each AZ's subnet. Instances mount via the nearest target; security groups control NFS access.
efs.simple: Each zone gets its own doorway into the well. Computers use the nearest one, and guards decide who gets in.

efs.a: Application-specific entry points that enforce a POSIX user and root directory, so each app or tenant sees only its own part of the file system.
efs.simple: Access points give each app its own door into the shared folder, so it only sees its own part.

efs.a: Elastic is the default: it scales automatically, you pay per use, and it suits spiky loads. Provisioned lets you set a level, and Bursting scales with stored size.
efs.simple: Elastic, the default, speeds up as needed and you pay per use. Or set a speed, or let it grow with size.

efs.q: When choose EFS One Zone over Regional?
efs.a: One Zone keeps data in one AZ for lower cost, which is fine for dev, build or staging data. Regional (recommended) spans AZs and survives an AZ loss.
efs.simple: One Zone is cheaper but keeps data in one place, fine for test data. Regional survives losing a zone.

efs.q: How does EFS replication help with disaster recovery?
efs.a: EFS keeps a copy of a file system's data and metadata in a destination file system and Region you choose, with a 15-minute recovery point objective for most file systems. To fail over, delete the replication configuration: the replica becomes writeable.
efs.simple: EFS can keep a copy of your shared drive in another place. If disaster strikes, you switch to the copy.

efs.q: How do you encrypt EFS traffic between your server and the file system?
efs.a: Mount with the EFS mount helper and its TLS option. It opens a secure TLS connection when the file system mounts, and all the file-sharing (NFS) traffic goes through it. Without the helper you can set up stunnel yourself.
efs.simple: Mount the shared drive with the EFS helper's encryption option, and everything sent to it is scrambled.

glue.a: Glue finds your data, cleans it and combines it so it's ready for analytics, machine learning (ML) or apps. It's serverless, so there are no clusters (groups of servers) to manage.
glue.simple: Gus finds your data, cleans it and joins it up so it's ready to use. There are no servers to manage.

glue.q: What is the AWS Glue Data Catalog?
glue.a: A central metadata store, like Gus's card index, that describes your databases and tables: each table's columns (schema), format and S3 location. Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR read it to query data in S3.
glue.simple: The Data Catalog is Gus's card index: it describes each table, its columns and where its files live.

glue.q: How do you pay for Glue jobs that tidy up data (ETL jobs)?
glue.a: By data processing units (DPUs), Glue's measure of computing power, for the time a job runs. You pay only while jobs run, with nothing for idle time.
glue.simple: You pay for the computer power a job uses, only while it runs. Waiting around is free.

glue.q: What does a Glue crawler do?
glue.a: Scans data stores such as S3, infers schemas and partitions, and creates or updates tables in the Data Catalog so data becomes queryable.
glue.simple: A crawler is a scout: it looks through your files, works out their shape and adds them to the catalog.

glue.q: What engine runs Glue ETL jobs?
glue.a: Serverless Apache Spark (Python or Scala), plus Python shell jobs for light tasks. You choose the worker type and count, and Glue provisions them and can auto scale.
glue.simple: Glue jobs run on Apache Spark, a big-data engine, with no servers for you to manage. Glue sets up the workers.

glue.a: State that tracks data already processed, so reruns of a job handle only new data instead of reprocessing everything.
glue.simple: Bookmarks remember what a job already did, so next time it only handles the new data.

glue.q: Why write partitioned Parquet from Glue?
glue.a: Columnar, compressed files partitioned by common filters (e.g. date) let Athena and Spark skip data, making queries faster and cheaper.
glue.simple: Saving data in neat column files, sorted into folders by date, lets questions skip what they don't need.

glue.q: What is AWS Glue Data Quality?
glue.a: Rules (in DQDL) that measure and monitor data quality in the catalog or in ETL jobs, so bad data can be flagged or stopped before it lands.
glue.simple: Data Quality rules check your data, so bad data can be flagged or stopped before it lands.

glue.q: When should a Glue job use the Flex execution class?
glue.a: For jobs that aren't urgent, like tests, pre-production runs and data loads. Flex runs on spare AWS capacity and cuts their cost by up to 35%, but start and run times can vary, so set a shorter timeout. It needs Glue 3.0 or later and no streaming.
glue.simple: Flex is the cheaper, slower lane: fine for jobs that can wait, not for ones that must finish on time.

glue.q: What does Auto Scaling do for a Glue job?
glue.a: With Glue 3.0 or later, Glue adds workers when a stage of the job needs more parallel work and removes idle ones, up to the maximum you set. You stop guessing the worker count and pay less for idle capacity.
glue.simple: Glue adds helpers when the job gets busy and sends them home when they're idle, so you don't guess the size.

athena.a: Athena lets you ask questions of files where they sit in S3, using standard SQL, the common database query language. There are no servers to run and no data to load first.
athena.simple: Thea shines her light on files right where they sit in S3 and answers your questions. Nothing to load first.

athena.q: How is Athena SQL priced by default?
athena.a: By how much data each query scans. Compressing files, splitting them into partitions (for example by date) and using columnar formats (stored by column) all mean less to scan, so queries cost less.
athena.simple: You pay for how much data each question reads. Smaller, tidier files mean cheaper questions.

athena.q: Where does Athena get table definitions?
athena.a: By default from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which records each table's schema, format and S3 location.
athena.simple: From the Glue Data Catalog, which records each table's shape, format and where its files live.

athena.a: Partitions (e.g. by year/month/day) let Athena read only matching folders when you filter on them, cutting both scan time and cost.
athena.simple: Sorting data into folders, like by date, lets Athena read only the folders you ask about: faster and cheaper.

athena.a: Separating users or teams: each can have its own query result location, encryption and per-query data-scan limits to control cost.
athena.simple: Workgroups give each team its own space, with its own results folder and spending limits.

athena.q: What does CTAS do in Athena?
athena.a: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT writes query results as a new table, e.g. converting CSV to partitioned Parquet in one step for cheaper future queries.
athena.simple: It saves a question's answer as a new table, for example turning messy files into tidy ones in one step.

athena.q: Why do Parquet/ORC formats reduce Athena cost?
athena.a: They are columnar and compressed, so Athena reads only the columns a query needs and skips row groups using statistics.
athena.simple: These formats store data by column and squeeze it small, so Athena reads only the columns it needs.

athena.a: It uses data source connectors to query sources beyond S3, like DynamoDB or relational databases, in place. You can join them in SQL, and many connectors run as Lambda functions.
athena.simple: Federated query lets Athena ask other databases too, right where they are, and mix the answers together.

athena.q: How can Athena answer a repeated query without scanning the data again?
athena.a: Turn on query result reuse and set a maximum age. If the same query ran in the same workgroup, its result hasn't expired and you can still read the tables and result location, Athena returns the stored result: faster, and no new bytes scanned.
athena.simple: Athena can hand back the answer it worked out last time, if it's fresh enough, so you don't pay to scan again.

athena.q: How can you update or delete single rows in an S3 data lake with Athena?
athena.a: Use ACID transactions on a shared table format such as Apache Iceberg. Athena then supports INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and time travel queries on S3 data, handles locking for concurrent users, and other engines like Spark can read the same tables.
athena.simple: Store the table as Iceberg and Athena can change or delete single rows safely, even look back in time.

lakeformation.a: Lars guards the data lake, a big store of raw data in S3. Lake Formation lets you control who can see which databases, tables and columns in the Data Catalog, all from one place.
lakeformation.simple: Lars guards the data lake gate and decides who can see which tables and columns, all from one place.

lakeformation.a: Instead of juggling many S3 bucket policies and IAM policies (permission rules), admins grant access to databases, tables and columns in one place. That also makes access easier to audit.
lakeformation.simple: One place to hand out data permissions beats many scattered rules, and it's easier to check later.

lakeformation.q: Does Lake Formation cost extra for permissions?
lakeformation.a: There's no additional charge for Lake Formation permissions. You pay for the underlying services, like S3, Glue and the engines that query data.
lakeformation.simple: Lake Formation permissions are free. You pay for the services that store and read the data.

lakeformation.q: What does registering an S3 location do?
lakeformation.a: Tells Lake Formation to manage access to that path, so integrated engines get temporary credentials based on Lake Formation grants.
lakeformation.simple: Registering a folder hands its keys to Lars, so tools reading it get short-lived passes based on his rules.

lakeformation.q: How do you restrict access to certain rows or columns?
lakeformation.a: Grant column-level permissions or create data filters for row- and cell-level security, so users see only what they are allowed to.
lakeformation.simple: Give permission to only some columns, or filter rows, so each person sees just what they're allowed to.

lakeformation.a: Tag-based access control: attach LF-Tags to databases, tables or columns and grant on tag expressions. Scales far better than per-table grants.
lakeformation.simple: Put labels on tables and columns, then grant by label. Much easier than granting table by table.

lakeformation.q: Which engines honour Lake Formation permissions?
lakeformation.a: Integrated services such as Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Amazon EMR and AWS Glue ETL enforce the grants when reading catalog tables.
lakeformation.simple: Athena, Glue and other connected tools follow Lars's rules when they read the catalog's tables.

lakeformation.q: How does Lake Formation share data across accounts?
lakeformation.a: Grant catalog resources to other accounts or an organisation (via AWS RAM). Consumers query in place without copying, enabling a data mesh.
lakeformation.simple: Share tables with other accounts so they can read them where they are, without copying anything.

lakeformation.q: What is a Lake Formation blueprint?
lakeformation.a: A template for loading data into your lake from a known kind of source, such as a relational database or CloudTrail logs. From it you create a workflow: Glue crawlers, jobs and triggers that load and update the data, tracked as one unit.
lakeformation.simple: A blueprint is a ready-made recipe for pulling data from a common source into your lake, on a schedule.

lakeformation.q: How can you move to Lake Formation permissions without breaking existing users?
lakeformation.a: Use hybrid access mode. You opt in chosen users and tables to Lake Formation permissions, and they then need both those and IAM permissions. Everyone else keeps their access through plain IAM policies until you move them.
lakeformation.simple: Hybrid mode moves people to the new permissions one group at a time, while everyone else keeps working.

dynamodb.a: A serverless NoSQL (non-relational) database. Its tables hold items you look up by a key, stored as key-value pairs or documents, with single-digit-millisecond reads and writes. On-demand mode needs no capacity planning.
dynamodb.simple: Give Dyna a card number and she fetches the card in a blink. A database with no servers that grows by itself.

dynamodb.q: What is the maximum size of a DynamoDB item?
dynamodb.a: 400 KB, counting both the field (attribute) names and their values. Put big files in S3 and store a pointer to them, such as the S3 key, in the item.
dynamodb.simple: One item can be up to 400 kilobytes. Keep big files in S3 and just write down where they are.

dynamodb.q: Pay per request or reserve it ahead (on-demand vs provisioned capacity)?
dynamodb.a: On-demand, the default and recommended mode, charges per read or write and scales by itself, even down to zero. Provisioned means you set reads and writes per second, helped by auto scaling, which suits steady, predictable traffic.
dynamodb.simple: On-demand, the usual choice, charges per read or write and grows by itself. Provisioned suits steady traffic.

dynamodb.q: Why does partition key choice matter?
dynamodb.a: DynamoDB spreads data across partitions by partition key hash. A high-cardinality key spreads traffic evenly. A skewed key creates hot partitions and throttling.
dynamodb.simple: The key decides which shelf each item goes on. Pick one that spreads items out, or one shelf gets swamped.

dynamodb.a: A GSI can use any partition and sort key and can be added any time. It has its own capacity, and its reads are eventually consistent. An LSI keeps the table's partition key, must be created with the table and allows strongly consistent reads.
dynamodb.simple: Indexes are extra card catalogues. A global one can be added any time; a local one must come with the table.

dynamodb.a: A time-ordered log of item-level changes, kept for 24 hours, in order per item. Lambda can process it to trigger workflows, update aggregates or replicate data.
dynamodb.simple: Streams are a diary of every change to your items, kept for a day, that Lambda can read and act on.

dynamodb.q: What does point-in-time recovery give you?
dynamodb.a: Automatic continuous backups. You can restore to any second in your recovery window, which is 1–35 days (default 35). A restore always creates a new table.
dynamodb.simple: It keeps backing up all the time, so you can rewind to any second in the last few weeks, as a new table.

dynamodb.a: Replicas of one table in several Regions, each serving reads and writes. The default, eventual consistency (MREC), copies changes within about a second, and the last write wins. Strong consistency (MRSC) uses exactly three Regions and always returns the latest data, but writes are slower.
dynamodb.simple: Global tables keep copies in several Regions, and each copy can be read and written. Changes spread fast.

dynamodb.q: How can DynamoDB delete old items for you, for free?
dynamodb.a: Turn on time to live (TTL) and store an expiry time on each item as a Number in Unix epoch seconds. DynamoDB deletes expired items, usually within a few days, without using write capacity. Filter expired items out of reads until then.
dynamodb.simple: Give each item an expiry time and DynamoDB deletes it for free a few days later. Good for old sessions.

dynamodb.q: When is DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) worth adding?
dynamodb.a: When single-digit milliseconds isn't fast enough. DAX is an in-memory cache with the DynamoDB API that cuts eventually consistent reads to microseconds, and it helps read-heavy or bursty apps that read the same keys again and again.
dynamodb.simple: This memory cache sits in front of DynamoDB and makes repeated reads super fast, with almost no code change.

rds.a: A managed service for relational databases, the classic kind made of tables. AWS sets them up, patches them, backs them up and switches to a spare if one fails, for MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2.
rds.simple: Ray keeps tidy ledgers of rows and columns. AWS sets up, patches and backs up these classic databases for you.

rds.a: A standby copy of your database in another Availability Zone, which takes over automatically during outages and maintenance. In a Multi-AZ DB instance the standby serves no reads, while a Multi-AZ DB cluster's two standbys can also serve reads.
rds.simple: A spare copy of your database waits in another zone and takes over by itself if the main one has trouble.

rds.a: Per instance hour, by size (instance class), On-Demand or discounted with Reserved Instances or Database Savings Plans. You also pay for storage, provisioned IOPS (reserved disk speed), data transfer and backups beyond the free allowance.
rds.simple: You pay per hour for the size of database you pick, plus its storage, extra speed and data sent out.

rds.q: What are RDS read replicas for?
rds.a: Asynchronously replicated copies that serve read traffic, offloading the primary. They can be in other Regions and can be promoted to standalone.
rds.simple: Read replicas are copies that answer read-only questions, so the main database has less to do.

rds.q: How long can automated RDS backups be kept?
rds.a: Up to 35 days. Setting it to 0 turns automated backups off. Point-in-time restore goes to any second in that window, up to about 5 minutes ago. The restore creates a new instance.
rds.simple: Automatic backups can be kept up to 35 days, and you can rewind to almost any second in that time.

rds.q: How should apps store RDS database passwords?
rds.a: In AWS Secrets Manager, or use IAM database authentication. Never put them in code. RDS can manage the master password in Secrets Manager and rotate it.
rds.simple: Never write passwords in your code. Keep them in a locked safe (Secrets Manager) that can change them for you.

rds.q: What does RDS Proxy help with?
rds.a: Pools and shares database connections, smoothing connection storms (e.g. from Lambda) and reducing failover time for applications.
rds.simple: The proxy shares a few database connections among many callers, so a sudden crowd doesn't overwhelm it.

rds.q: What does Performance Insights / Database Insights show?
rds.a: Database load broken down by waits, SQL, hosts and users, so you can find which queries cause bottlenecks before scaling hardware.
rds.simple: It shows what's keeping your database busy, so you can fix slow questions before buying a bigger one.

rds.q: Multi-AZ DB instance or Multi-AZ DB cluster: what's the difference?
rds.a: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readable replicas in three Availability Zones, with semisynchronous replication. Compared with a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, it adds read capacity and lowers write latency.
rds.simple: A cluster keeps two spare copies in other zones that can also answer reads, so it's faster as well as safer.

rds.q: How do RDS Blue/Green Deployments make database upgrades safer?
rds.a: RDS makes a staging copy (green) that stays in sync with production (blue). You upgrade the engine or change parameters on green and test it, then switch over, usually in under a minute with no data loss and no app changes.
rds.simple: RDS builds a twin of your database to try changes on, then swaps it in within about a minute.

aurora.a: A relational database built for the cloud that works with MySQL and PostgreSQL. Its storage is spread across many machines, so it handles more work (throughput) and stays available.
aurora.simple: Rory's database works with MySQL and PostgreSQL but is built for the cloud, so it does more work and stays up.

aurora.q: How does Aurora store data durably?
aurora.a: Aurora's shared storage (the cluster volume) keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones (separate groups of data centres). Your data survives losing some storage machines, or even a whole AZ.
aurora.simple: Aurora keeps six copies of your data across three zones, so it survives even if a whole zone is lost.

aurora.q: Does Aurora storage need to be pre-provisioned?
aurora.a: No. Aurora storage grows automatically as data is added, and you pay for what is used, so no capacity planning for disks.
aurora.simple: No. Its storage grows by itself as you add data, and you pay for what you use.

aurora.q: Writer vs reader endpoint in Aurora?
aurora.a: The cluster (writer) endpoint points to the primary for writes. The reader endpoint load-balances connections across Aurora Replicas for reads.
aurora.simple: One address is for writing, to the main copy. The reader address shares reading among the helper copies.

aurora.q: How many Aurora Replicas can a cluster have?
aurora.a: Up to 15 Aurora Replicas sharing the same storage volume. They scale reads and act as failover targets for the writer.
aurora.simple: Up to 15 helper copies share the same storage. They answer reads and can take over if the writer fails.

aurora.a: Capacity is measured in Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs). It scales with load in steps as small as 0.5 ACU. On recent engine versions it can pause at 0 ACUs when idle. It suits variable workloads.
aurora.simple: Aurora Serverless grows and shrinks in small steps as work comes and goes, and can even pause when idle.

aurora.a: Clones share storage copy-on-write, so creating a test copy of a large database is fast and cheap until data diverges.
aurora.simple: A clone is a quick, cheap copy for testing: it shares the same storage until either copy changes.

aurora.q: What does Aurora Global Database provide?
aurora.a: One primary Region plus read-only secondary Regions. Data replicates at the storage layer, typically with sub-second lag. That gives you local reads and cross-Region DR.
aurora.simple: One main Region plus read-only copies in others, updated in about a second, for local reads and recovery.

aurora.a: A serverless, distributed SQL database for transactional apps that works with PostgreSQL drivers and tools. There are no servers to manage, and it scales compute, I/O and storage with your workload.
aurora.simple: A newer Aurora with no servers to manage. It grows with your app and works with PostgreSQL tools.

aurora.q: How available is Aurora DSQL, and how do multi-Region clusters work?
aurora.a: 99.99% in one Region and 99.999% across Regions. Peered clusters give you an endpoint in each Region. Both take reads and writes and show one consistent database.
aurora.simple: Built to stay up 99.99% of the time in one Region and 99.999% across Regions, where every Region takes writes.

aurora.q: What happens when two Aurora DSQL transactions change the same row?
aurora.a: DSQL uses optimistic concurrency control instead of locks. Conflicts are checked at commit: the first to commit wins and the other gets error 40001 (OC000), so your app should retry it.
aurora.simple: There are no locks. If two changes clash, the first to finish wins and the other must try again.

elasticache.a: Cara keeps popular orders ready: ElastiCache holds data in memory as a fast cache, answering reads in microseconds to milliseconds. It works with Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, popular open-source in-memory engines.
elasticache.simple: Cara keeps regulars' orders ready on the counter: answers served from fast memory, in a blink.

elasticache.q: Why put a cache in front of a database?
elasticache.a: Common requests are answered from fast memory, so users wait less (lower latency) and the database does less work. You can then serve more users with a smaller database.
elasticache.simple: Popular answers come from fast memory, so people wait less and the database has less work to do.

elasticache.a: A way to run ElastiCache that grows and shrinks on its own, with no servers (nodes) to size. You pay per GB-hour of data stored (each GB, each hour) and per ECPU (ElastiCache Processing Unit) used.
elasticache.simple: Serverless ElastiCache grows and shrinks by itself. You pay for data kept and work done, no sizes to pick.

elasticache.q: What is the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern?
elasticache.a: The app checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads the database and writes the result to the cache. Only requested data is cached.
elasticache.simple: Check the counter first. If the order isn't there, ask the kitchen, then keep a copy on the counter.

elasticache.q: Why set a TTL on cached items?
elasticache.a: A time to live expires stale entries automatically, bounding how out of date data can get and keeping memory for hot keys.
elasticache.simple: A time to live is a sell-by date: old answers expire by themselves, so the cache never gets too stale.

elasticache.q: What does cluster mode enabled give Valkey/Redis OSS?
elasticache.a: Data is partitioned across many shards, each with a primary and up to 5 replicas. The default limit is 90 nodes per cluster, and a quota increase allows up to 500. Memory and writes scale beyond one primary.
elasticache.simple: Cluster mode splits data into many pieces, each with helpers, so memory and writes grow past one machine.

elasticache.q: How do you make a Valkey/Redis OSS cache highly available?
elasticache.a: Use replicas in other AZs with Multi-AZ automatic failover, so a replica is promoted if the primary fails.
elasticache.simple: Keep helper copies in other zones. If the main one fails, a helper takes over by itself.

elasticache.q: Which Valkey/Redis data type suits a live leaderboard?
elasticache.a: Sorted sets: members are kept ordered by score, so rank and top-N queries are fast without sorting in the application.
elasticache.simple: Sorted sets keep players in score order, so the top ten comes back fast without sorting yourself.

elasticache.q: Memcached or Valkey/Redis OSS: which ElastiCache engine?
elasticache.a: Memcached for the simplest model: caching objects, large multi-threaded nodes, adding and removing nodes freely. Valkey or Redis OSS for rich data types, replication and failover, and newer features such as vector search.
elasticache.simple: Memcached is a plain, simple cache. Valkey does much more: lists, rankings, backup copies and search.

elasticache.q: What does an ElastiCache global datastore give you?
elasticache.a: Valkey or Redis OSS replication across Regions: one primary cluster takes writes, and read-only secondary clusters in other Regions copy it asynchronously. You get fast local reads far away, and can promote a secondary if the primary degrades.
elasticache.simple: A copy of your cache in another Region: nearby users read faster, and it can take over in a disaster.

redshift.a: A managed data warehouse, a database built for analysing large amounts of data (OLAP). It stores data by column and splits big SQL queries across many machines at once (massively parallel processing).
redshift.simple: Reggie's huge warehouse stores billions of rows by column, so big questions about lots of data come back fast.

redshift.q: Everyday sales or big-picture reports (OLTP vs OLAP): where does Redshift fit?
redshift.a: OLAP. Redshift answers big questions over lots of past data. Apps doing many small reads and writes, like orders or logins (OLTP), belong in RDS, Aurora or DynamoDB.
redshift.simple: Redshift is for big-picture questions about lots of past data. Everyday small orders belong elsewhere.

redshift.a: Redshift with no clusters to manage, where capacity scales on its own. Compute is billed in RPU-hours (Redshift Processing Units), per second with a 60-second minimum and only while in use, and storage is billed separately.
redshift.simple: Redshift Serverless grows by itself, and you pay for computing only while it's busy, per second.

redshift.q: How does Redshift query data in S3 without loading it?
redshift.a: With external tables, for example from the Glue Data Catalog, which you can join with warehouse tables. RA3 and DC2 clusters use Redshift Spectrum. Serverless and RG clusters use a built-in lake engine.
redshift.simple: External tables let Redshift read files in S3 without loading them, and mix them with its own tables.

redshift.q: How do you bulk-load data into Redshift efficiently?
redshift.a: Use COPY from S3 or other sources. It loads in parallel across slices. Uncompressed CSV, Parquet and ORC files of 128 MB or more split automatically. Split compressed or JSON input yourself into similar-size files, a multiple of the slice count.
redshift.simple: The copy command loads many files at once in parallel. Split big data into similar-size files to help it.

redshift.a: They decide how rows are spread across nodes (AUTO, EVEN, KEY, ALL). Co-locating join keys avoids shuffling data between nodes during queries.
redshift.simple: They decide how rows are spread over the machines. Keeping matching rows together saves passing data around.

redshift.a: They order data on disk, so range filters can use zone maps to skip blocks. That speeds up queries that filter on things like dates.
redshift.simple: Sort keys keep data in order, like dates, so questions can skip whole chunks they don't need.

redshift.q: Why use materialized views in Redshift?
redshift.a: They store precomputed results of expensive queries and can refresh incrementally, giving dashboards fast answers at lower compute cost.
redshift.simple: They keep ready-made answers to hard questions, so dashboards get answers fast and cheaply.

redshift.q: How does Redshift cope when thousands of users query at once?
redshift.a: Turn on concurrency scaling. Redshift adds cluster capacity on its own for spikes in read queries and common writes such as ETL, so eligible queries don't wait in a queue. Users still see current data, and you pay only while the extra capacity runs queries.
redshift.simple: When lots of people ask at once, Redshift adds extra helpers for a while, and you pay only while they work.

redshift.q: How can another team query your Redshift data without a copy?
redshift.a: Use data sharing. It gives live access to your tables across clusters, Serverless workgroups, AWS accounts and Regions, with no copying or moving. Readers see updates as soon as a write commits, and you control what each one may read or write.
redshift.simple: Share your tables directly: other teams see the live data, always up to date, without making copies.

neptune.a: Neptune is a managed graph database, for data that is all about connections. It stores things (nodes, or vertices) and the links between them (edges), and quickly follows paths from one to another.
neptune.simple: Nep weaves a web of who knows whom. Neptune stores things and the links between them, and follows paths fast.

neptune.q: When is a graph database a better fit?
neptune.a: When the connections matter most, as in social networks, fraud rings, recommendations and knowledge graphs. Questions like "friends of friends of friends" are slow joins in SQL but simple walks (traversals) in a graph.
neptune.simple: When connections matter most, like friends of friends or fraud rings, a web is easier to walk than tables.

neptune.a: Yes. Neptune Serverless scales capacity automatically with demand. A cluster can mix serverless and provisioned instances, using provisioned ones for steady workloads.
neptune.simple: Yes. Neptune Serverless grows and shrinks with demand, and you can mix it with fixed-size machines.

neptune.q: Which query languages does Neptune support?
neptune.a: Apache TinkerPop Gremlin and openCypher for property graphs, and SPARQL for RDF graphs.
neptune.simple: It speaks three graph languages: Gremlin and openCypher for one kind of web, and another for linked-data webs.

neptune.q: How does Neptune store data for durability?
neptune.a: On a shared cluster volume copied across three AZs. The volume self-heals and survives losing copies. Up to 15 read replicas can scale reads.
neptune.simple: Copies are kept across three zones and fix themselves, and up to 15 helper copies can answer reads.

neptune.q: How does a graph help fraud detection?
neptune.a: Fraudsters share IP addresses, cards or emails. Traversing those links in near real time reveals rings of related accounts that row-by-row checks miss.
neptune.simple: Cheats often share cards, emails or addresses. Following those links reveals whole rings of linked accounts.

neptune.q: Why keep Neptune in private subnets?
neptune.a: Neptune always runs in your VPC. Private subnets with public access left off keep it off the internet. Security groups and IAM auth control who can connect.
neptune.simple: Neptune always lives in your private network. Private rooms keep it off the internet; guards check visitors.

neptune.q: What is Neptune Analytics used for with GenAI?
neptune.a: An analytics graph engine with vector search. It can back GraphRAG in Bedrock Knowledge Bases, linking entities to improve answer relevance.
neptune.simple: Neptune Analytics can link facts together so an AI's answers find the right, related information.

neptune.q: Property graph or RDF: how do Neptune's two graph models differ?
neptune.a: In a property graph, nodes and edges can each carry extra properties, and you query with Gremlin or openCypher. RDF stores facts as triples (subject, predicate, object), each part named by a URI, and you query with SPARQL, a web standard.
neptune.simple: Two graph styles: dots and lines that carry details, or simple three-part facts like 'Ana knows Bo'.

neptune.q: Neptune Database or Neptune Analytics: which one?
neptune.a: Neptune Database serves live apps such as social networks, fraud alerts and Customer 360, up to 100,000 queries a second with Multi-AZ and multi-Region options. Neptune Analytics loads big graphs into memory to run graph algorithms for insights and trends.
neptune.simple: Neptune Database runs your live app. Neptune Analytics studies a huge graph in memory to spot patterns.

vpc.a: Your own private network inside AWS, walled off from everyone else's, like Vic's walled garden. You pick its range of IP addresses and split it into smaller plots called subnets.
vpc.simple: Your own walled garden in the cloud, like Vic's. You choose its addresses and split it into small plots.

vpc.a: Its route table (the subnet's list of directions) sends traffic for all addresses (0.0.0.0/0) to an internet gateway, the network's door to the internet. Private subnets have no such route, so the internet can't reach them directly.
vpc.simple: A public plot has a path to the internet's gate. Private plots have none, so the internet can't walk in.

vpc.q: Can a subnet span multiple Availability Zones?
vpc.a: No. Each subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone (AZ), a separate group of data centres within a Region. To keep running if one AZ fails, put subnets in at least two AZs and spread your resources across them.
vpc.simple: No. Each plot lives in one zone. Put plots in at least two zones so you keep running if one zone fails.

vpc.a: Security groups are stateful, allow-only, and attach to resources. NACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, evaluate rules in order, and apply per subnet.
vpc.simple: Security groups guard each resource and remember replies. Network lists guard a whole plot and can say no.

vpc.q: What does a NAT gateway do?
vpc.a: Lets resources in private subnets start outbound connections (e.g. for updates) while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. It is billed hourly and per GB processed.
vpc.simple: A one-way door: private things can go out to fetch updates, but strangers can't come in. You pay for its use.

vpc.q: Why use gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB?
vpc.a: Traffic reaches S3/DynamoDB over the AWS network without an internet or NAT gateway. Gateway endpoints have no extra charge, saving NAT data costs.
vpc.simple: They're a private path to S3 and DynamoDB that skips the internet, and they cost nothing extra.

vpc.q: How many IP addresses does AWS reserve in each subnet?
vpc.a: Five: the first four and the last address of the subnet CIDR (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast). Plan subnet sizes accordingly.
vpc.simple: Five addresses in every plot are kept for AWS's own use, so plan your plot sizes with that in mind.

vpc.a: Peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link. Transit Gateway is a hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks, simplifying routing at scale.
vpc.simple: Peering is a private lane between two networks. Transit Gateway is a hub that links many networks together.

vpc.q: What do VPC Flow Logs record, and do they slow your network?
vpc.a: They capture information about the IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC, sent to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Data Firehose. Use them to debug security group rules that are too strict or see what reaches an instance. They're collected outside the traffic path, so no slowdown.
vpc.simple: Flow logs note who talked to whom in your network, without slowing it. Great for finding blocked traffic.

vpc.q: Gateway endpoint or interface endpoint: how do you reach AWS services privately?
vpc.a: Gateway endpoints serve only S3 and DynamoDB, at no extra charge. Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) put network interfaces with private IP addresses in your subnets for many more services, without an internet gateway, billed per hour per Availability Zone plus per GB.
vpc.simple: Private doors to AWS services: free ones for S3 and DynamoDB, paid ones for almost everything else.

route53.a: It runs DNS, the internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address of a server. It can also register domain names and check that your servers are healthy.
route53.simple: Ruby calls out addresses: Route 53 is the internet's phone book, turning names into server addresses.

route53.a: A folder of DNS records for one domain, such as where www.example.com points. A public zone answers anyone on the internet. A private zone answers only inside the VPCs you link to it.
route53.simple: A hosted zone is a folder of address cards for one website name. Public ones answer anyone, private ones you.

route53.a: A monthly fee for each hosted zone, plus a small charge per DNS lookup (query). Registering a domain costs extra, and up to 50 health checks on AWS endpoints are free.
route53.simple: A small monthly fee per folder of address cards, plus a tiny charge per lookup. Website names cost extra.

route53.q: Why use an alias record instead of a CNAME?
route53.a: Alias records can point the zone apex (example.com) at AWS resources like CloudFront or a load balancer. CNAMEs cannot. Aliases also track the resource's IP changes.
route53.simple: An alias can point your bare website name straight at AWS things, and follows them if their address changes.

route53.a: Weighted (split traffic by ratio), latency (send to lowest-latency Region) and failover (active-passive). Others: simple, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue and IP-based.
route53.simple: Weighted shares visitors out, latency sends them to the fastest Region, and failover switches to a spare.

route53.q: How do health checks enable DNS failover?
route53.a: Route 53 checks endpoints and, when the primary fails, stops returning it and answers with the secondary record instead.
route53.simple: Route 53 checks if your servers are well. If the main one is sick, it sends visitors to the backup instead.

route53.q: What does Route 53 DNSSEC signing protect against?
route53.a: It lets resolvers verify responses came from your zone unaltered, defending against DNS spoofing (forged responses).
route53.simple: It adds a signature to your address cards, so nobody can trick visitors with fake ones.

route53.q: What does Route 53 VPC Resolver (formerly Route 53 Resolver) provide for hybrid networks?
route53.a: Inbound and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules so VPCs and on-premises DNS can resolve each other's private names.
route53.simple: It lets your cloud network and your office network look up each other's private names.

route53.q: Which DNS record types will you meet most often?
route53.a: A (an IPv4 address), AAAA (an IPv6 address), CNAME (one name pointing at another, not allowed at the zone apex), MX (mail servers) and TXT (text, often for verification). Route 53 adds alias records, which point at AWS resources and work at the apex.
route53.simple: Each address card has a type: some hold a computer's address, some point to a name, some say where mail goes.

route53.q: Latency or geolocation routing: when do you use which?
route53.a: Latency routing sends each user to the Region that answers them fastest. Geolocation routing picks the resource by where the user is: show content in their language or only where you have rights. Add a default record for locations Route 53 can't place.
route53.simple: Latency sends people to the quickest place. Geolocation sends them by country, say for their own language.

cloudfront.a: A content delivery network (CDN): Cleo keeps copies of your content at edge locations, AWS sites in cities around the world. Users get it from a nearby site, so it loads faster.
cloudfront.simple: Cleo keeps copies of your website in post offices worldwide, so every visitor gets it from nearby, fast.

cloudfront.q: What is an origin in CloudFront?
cloudfront.a: The place CloudFront gets the original content from, such as an S3 bucket (AWS object storage) or any web server. When an edge location doesn't have a copy yet, it fetches one from the origin.
cloudfront.simple: The origin is where the original lives, like an S3 bucket. A post office without a copy fetches one there.

cloudfront.q: Why does CloudFront often lower cost as well as latency?
cloudfront.a: When an edge location already has a copy, it answers without asking your origin, so the origin does less work and sends less data. Moving data from an AWS origin to CloudFront is free.
cloudfront.simple: When a nearby post office already has a copy, your origin does less work, so it costs less too.

cloudfront.a: Lets CloudFront sign requests to a private S3 bucket so the bucket stays non-public and only the distribution can read it. Recommended over legacy OAI.
cloudfront.simple: It lets only CloudFront open your private bucket, so the bucket never has to be public.

cloudfront.q: How do you make new content appear before the TTL expires?
cloudfront.a: Create an invalidation for the paths, or better, version file names (app.v2.js) so each deploy uses new cache keys.
cloudfront.simple: Tell post offices to throw out old copies, or better, give each new file version a new name.

cloudfront.q: What do cache behaviours let you do?
cloudfront.a: Apply different origins, TTLs, cache policies and functions per path pattern. For example, cache static assets for a long time but pass API paths straight through.
cloudfront.simple: Different paths get different rules, like keeping pictures for ages but always fetching fresh data.

cloudfront.a: Both restrict private content. Signed URLs suit single files; signed cookies grant access to many files (e.g. a video library) without changing URLs.
cloudfront.simple: Both are passes for private content. A signed link opens one file; a signed cookie opens many.

cloudfront.a: CloudFront Functions are lightweight JavaScript for sub-millisecond header or URL tweaks at scale. Lambda@Edge handles heavier logic, network calls and origin events.
cloudfront.simple: CloudFront Functions do tiny, super-fast tweaks. Lambda@Edge handles bigger jobs that need more time.

cloudfront.q: What is a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan?
cloudfront.a: One monthly price that bundles CloudFront with AWS WAF, DDoS protection, Route 53 DNS, a TLS certificate and S3 storage credits. Plans come in Free, Pro, Business and Premium, with no annual commitment.
cloudfront.simple: One monthly price that bundles CloudFront with protection, a website name service, a certificate and storage.

cloudfront.q: What if a CloudFront flat-rate plan goes over its usage allowance?
cloudfront.a: You never pay overage charges. Allowances aren't hard limits: you get emails at 50%, 80% and 100%. Only sustained or very large excess may slow delivery until you upgrade.
cloudfront.simple: You're never charged extra. You get emails as you near the limit, and only huge, lasting excess may slow it.

cloudfront.q: Do DDoS attacks use up a CloudFront flat-rate plan’s allowance?
cloudfront.a: No. Blocked DDoS attacks and requests that AWS WAF blocks never count. Only traffic that gets past your WAF rules counts toward the monthly allowance.
cloudfront.simple: No. Attacks that get blocked never count. Only traffic that gets past your guard rules counts.

apigateway.a: A managed front door for your APIs, the web addresses other programs call to use your app. Gabe takes each request and sends it on to Lambda (code that runs on demand), a web server or another AWS service.
apigateway.simple: Gabe's station is the front door for apps: each request has its ticket checked and is sent the right way.

apigateway.q: Which API types does API Gateway offer?
apigateway.a: Three kinds. REST APIs have the most features, HTTP APIs are simpler and cheaper, and WebSocket APIs keep a connection open so both sides can send messages in real time.
apigateway.simple: Three kinds: one with the most features, a simpler cheaper one, and one that keeps a line open to chat.

apigateway.a: No minimum fee. REST and HTTP APIs charge per million calls plus data sent out. WebSocket APIs charge per million messages plus minutes connected.
apigateway.simple: No minimum fee. You pay per million calls or messages, plus data sent out or time connected.

apigateway.q: What is a Lambda proxy integration?
apigateway.a: API Gateway passes the whole request to Lambda as an event and returns the function's response, keeping routing logic simple.
apigateway.simple: The station hands the whole request to Lambda and passes back its answer, keeping things simple.

apigateway.q: Default account throttle limit per Region?
apigateway.a: 10,000 requests per second with a burst of 5,000, lower in some newer Regions. You can request a higher RPS quota. Add stage or method throttles, and usage plans for per-client limits.
apigateway.simple: By default about 10,000 requests a second per Region, with short bursts allowed. You can ask for more.

apigateway.q: How can you authorise API Gateway requests?
