apigateway.a: IAM (SigV4), Cognito user pool authorizers on REST APIs, JWT authorizers on HTTP APIs, or Lambda authorizers for custom logic. Check tokens at the gateway, not in every function.
apigateway.simple: Check each pass once at the station gate, not in every function: with Cognito, IAM or your own checker.

apigateway.q: What are usage plans and API keys for?
apigateway.a: REST API features to meter and throttle individual clients and set quotas. API keys identify clients but are not a replacement for authorization.
apigateway.simple: Usage plans give each customer their own limits. Keys say who's calling, but they aren't proper locks.

apigateway.q: What are stages and why use them?
apigateway.a: A stage is a named reference (dev, prod) to a deployment, which is a snapshot of the API. Each stage has its own settings, variables, logging and throttles. This enables safe promotion and canaries.
apigateway.simple: A stage is a named copy, like test or live, each with its own settings, so you can try changes safely.

apigateway.q: What can a Lambda authorizer return besides an allow or deny policy?
apigateway.a: A context map of strings, numbers or booleans (no objects or arrays). API Gateway exposes it as $context.authorizer values, and a Lambda proxy integration receives it in the event, for example the caller's tenant id.
apigateway.simple: Extra facts about the caller, like which company they belong to, passed on to your code.

apigateway.q: How can a Lambda authorizer pick a caller's usage plan?
apigateway.a: Set the API's key source to AUTHORIZER, and have the authorizer return one of the usage plan's API keys as usageIdentifierKey. Throttles and quotas then apply per key, on a best-effort basis.
apigateway.simple: The authorizer names the caller's key, so each customer gets their own speed limit.

apigateway.q: Should API keys be used to decide who may call an API?
apigateway.a: No. API keys with usage plans meter and throttle clients on a best-effort basis, but AWS advises against using them for authentication, authorization or cost control. Use authorizers for access, and AWS WAF and AWS Budgets for cost.
apigateway.simple: No. Keys count and slow down callers, but a proper sign-in check must decide who gets in.

sqs.a: A message queue that AWS runs for you, like Quinn's post office. One part of your app drops off messages and another picks them up when it's ready, so if one part slows down or fails, the other keeps going.
sqs.simple: Letters wait in Quinn's queue until someone is ready, so if one part of your app is slow, the rest carries on.

sqs.a: A publish/subscribe service: you send a message to a topic once, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber. Subscribers can be SQS queues, Lambda functions, email addresses or phones by SMS text.
sqs.simple: SNS is the bell: ring once and every subscriber hears it, whether a queue, a function, an email or a phone.

sqs.q: How long does SQS keep messages?
sqs.a: 4 days by default, configurable from 60 seconds up to 14 days. Consumers must delete a message after processing it.
sqs.simple: Four days by default, and anywhere from one minute up to 14 days. Delete each message once you've handled it.

sqs.a: Standard gives nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery and best-effort order. FIFO keeps order per message group and gives exactly-once processing, with lower throughput. Its deduplication window is 5 minutes.
sqs.simple: Standard is fast and roomy but may mix up the order or repeat. First-in-first-out keeps order, once each.

sqs.a: After a consumer receives a message, the message is hidden (default 30 s, max 12 h). If it isn't deleted in time, it reappears for retry. Set the timeout above your processing time.
sqs.simple: A picked-up message hides for a while. If it isn't finished and deleted in time, it comes back to retry.

sqs.a: A queue for messages that were received maxReceiveCount times without being deleted. It isolates poison messages so you can inspect and redrive them.
sqs.simple: Messages that keep failing go to a separate queue, so they don't block the line and you can look later.

sqs.a: ReceiveMessage waits up to 20 seconds for messages instead of returning empty, reducing empty responses and request cost.
sqs.simple: Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for a letter instead of checking an empty box again and again. Cheaper!

sqs.q: What is the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern?
sqs.a: Publish once to an SNS topic that several SQS queues subscribe to. Each consumer gets its own durable copy and scales independently. Filter policies route subsets of messages.
sqs.simple: Ring the bell once and several queues each get their own copy, so each helper works at its own pace.

sqs.q: How big can an SQS message be, and what if yours is bigger?
sqs.a: Up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). For more, the SQS Extended Client Library for Java or Python stores the payload in S3, up to 2 GB, and sends a message holding a pointer to it.
sqs.simple: A message holds up to 1 MiB. For bigger things, put the file in S3 and send a note saying where it is.

sqs.q: Delay queue or visibility timeout: what's the difference?
sqs.a: Both hide messages for a while. A delay queue hides each new message when it's first added, for up to 15 minutes. A visibility timeout hides a message only after a consumer receives it. For scheduling further ahead, use EventBridge Scheduler.
sqs.simple: A delay hides a new message before anyone sees it. A visibility timeout hides it while a worker handles it.

sqs.q: How fast can an SQS FIFO queue go?
sqs.a: Without high throughput mode, 300 calls per second per action, or 3,000 messages a second with batches of 10. High throughput mode raises that a lot, up to 70,000 calls a second in the largest Regions. Spread messages across many message group IDs to use it.
sqs.simple: Ordered queues are slower than standard ones. Batching and high throughput mode speed them up a lot.

eventbridge.a: A serverless router for events, small notes that something happened, like 'file uploaded'. It sends events from AWS services, SaaS apps (other companies' software) and your own code to the targets you pick.
eventbridge.simple: Eve watches events, little notes that something happened, and sends each one to whoever cares.

eventbridge.a: A router that receives events. Each account has a default bus for AWS service events. You can create custom buses for your own applications.
eventbridge.simple: An event bus is the railway line events travel on. Each account has one for AWS, and you can add your own.

eventbridge.a: Pay as you go, with no minimum fee. On a classic bus, AWS service events arrive free and you pay per million for your own or partner events. The newer Custom Event Bus bills for the data you publish, deliver and keep.
eventbridge.simple: No minimum fee. Events from AWS services arrive free on the classic bus, and your own events cost a little.

eventbridge.q: What is an event pattern in a rule?
eventbridge.a: A JSON filter matching fields such as source and detail-type. Only matching events are sent to the rule's targets, like Lambda or SQS.
eventbridge.simple: A pattern is a filter: only events that match it, like 'file uploaded', go on to the rule's targets.

eventbridge.a: Creating cron, rate or one-time schedules that invoke many AWS targets, with time zones and retries, without running your own scheduler.
eventbridge.simple: The scheduler is an alarm clock for the cloud: it runs jobs on a timetable, or just once, with no server.

eventbridge.a: Connect a source (e.g. SQS, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis) to a target point-to-point with optional filtering and enrichment, replacing glue code.
eventbridge.simple: Pipes join one source straight to one target, filtering and adding details on the way, with no extra code.

eventbridge.a: On a classic bus, an archive keeps events and a replay sends them back to that same bus. Use this to recover from bugs or test new code. The newer Custom Event Bus keeps events itself, so a subscriber replays them by starting from an earlier point.
eventbridge.simple: Keep a recording of events and play it back later, to recover from mistakes or test new code.

eventbridge.a: EventBridge offers rich content filtering, SaaS sources, schema registry and replay. SNS suits very high fan-out at lower latency and pushes to mobile, SMS and email.
eventbridge.simple: EventBridge has smarter filters and replay. SNS is faster for huge crowds and can text, email and buzz phones.

eventbridge.q: What happens when EventBridge can't deliver an event to a target?
eventbridge.a: It retries with exponential back-off and random jitter, by default for 24 hours and up to 185 times; you can change both in the target's retry policy. After that the event is dropped, so attach a dead-letter queue to keep failed events.
eventbridge.simple: EventBridge keeps trying for up to a day, then gives up, unless a spare queue catches what it missed.

eventbridge.q: How do you send events from one AWS account's bus to another's?
eventbridge.a: On the receiving account, add a resource policy to its event bus that lets chosen accounts, or your whole organisation, send events. On the sending account, create a rule whose target is that bus. Then the receiver's own rules route the events onward.
eventbridge.simple: Let the other account accept your events, then add a rule that forwards events to its bus.

iam.a: Identity and Access Management controls who is authenticated (signed in) and authorised (has permissions) to use AWS resources. There is no extra charge for IAM.
iam.simple: Ivy checks every badge: who you are, and exactly what you're allowed to do. It's free.

iam.q: Why should you not use the root user for daily tasks?
iam.a: The root user, the account's first login, can do everything, and you can't attach IAM policies (permission rules) to it. Turn on MFA (a second sign-in code), create no access keys for it, and use it only for the few tasks that need it.
iam.simple: The root user can do everything, which makes it risky. Lock it with a second sign-in code and use it rarely.

iam.q: A permanent login or a borrowed badge (IAM user vs role)?
iam.a: An IAM user has a lasting password or access keys. A role hands out short-lived credentials to whoever takes it on (assumes it). AWS recommends roles for apps, and sign-in through IAM Identity Center (federation) for people.
iam.simple: A user is a permanent login. A role is a borrowed badge that expires soon, which is safer for apps and people.

iam.a: Grant only the actions, resources and conditions a task needs. Then tighten broad permissions over time. IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies and find unused access, and last-accessed data helps too.
iam.simple: Least privilege: give only the exact permissions a job needs, nothing more, and trim extras over time.

iam.q: How does IAM evaluate an allow vs an explicit deny?
iam.a: Every request is denied by default, except for the root user. An allow works only if no SCP, RCP, boundary or session policy blocks it. An explicit deny in any applicable policy always wins.
iam.simple: Everything starts as a no. An allow opens the door, but any clear 'deny' always wins.

iam.q: How is cross-account access usually granted?
iam.a: Create a role in the target account whose trust policy trusts the other account. Principals in that account who are allowed sts:AssumeRole on the role can assume it and get temporary credentials.
iam.simple: Make a role in one account that trusts the other account, so its people can borrow that badge for a while.

iam.a: A managed policy that caps the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can have. It grants nothing itself. Useful to let developers create roles without escalating privilege.
iam.simple: A boundary is a fence: it sets the most a user or role could ever do, but gives no permissions itself.

iam.q: Do Service Control Policies grant permissions?
iam.a: No. SCPs only cap the maximum permissions for users and roles in member accounts. They don't affect the management account. Access must still be granted by identity-based or resource-based policies.
iam.simple: No. They are a ceiling for whole accounts. Permissions still have to be given by normal policies.

iam.a: A policy you pass when you assume a role, for example with aws sts assume-role --policy. The session's permissions are the intersection of the role's policies and the session policy, so it can only narrow access, never widen it.
iam.simple: An extra rule added when you borrow a role. It can only take permissions away, never add them.

iam.q: How does the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition help keep tenants apart?
iam.a: It checks the partition key values a request touches. A policy with ForAllValues:StringEquals on dynamodb:LeadingKeys set to one tenant id only allows that tenant's items, so a bug can't read another tenant's rows.
iam.simple: It lets a request touch only rows whose key belongs to its own customer.

cognito.a: Coco handles sign-up and sign-in for your app's users, including MFA (a second code) and 'Sign in with Google'-style logins. After sign-in, Cognito gives the app tokens, signed passes your server can check.
cognito.simple: Coco runs the passport office: sign-up, sign-in and second codes, then hands your app a signed pass.

cognito.q: A sign-in list or an AWS access pass (user pool vs identity pool)?
cognito.a: A user pool is a list of your users that checks their sign-ins and issues JWTs (signed sign-in tokens). An identity pool swaps a user's identity for temporary AWS credentials, so the app can call AWS directly.
cognito.simple: A user pool is your list of users and checks their sign-ins. An identity pool swaps that for a short AWS pass.

cognito.q: How is Cognito user pool usage priced?
cognito.a: Mainly by monthly active users. Feature plans (Lite, Essentials, Plus) add capabilities, such as threat protection (formerly advanced security), at higher tiers.
cognito.simple: Mostly by how many users sign in each month. Higher plans add extra features, like better security.

cognito.q: What tokens does a user pool issue?
cognito.a: An ID token (who the user is), an access token (what they can call) and a refresh token (to get new tokens without signing in again).
cognito.simple: Three passes: one says who you are, one says what you may use, and one gets fresh passes without signing in.

cognito.q: What is managed login in Cognito?
cognito.a: Hosted, customisable sign-in pages with OAuth 2.0/OIDC endpoints, so you get sign-up, sign-in and social login without building auth UI.
cognito.simple: Ready-made sign-in pages you can style, so you don't have to build sign-up and sign-in screens yourself.

cognito.q: How do you protect an API with Cognito?
cognito.a: Use an API Gateway Cognito user pool or JWT authorizer so tokens are validated (signature, expiry, issuer, scopes) before your backend runs.
cognito.simple: Let the API Gateway station check each pass is real and fresh before your code even runs.

cognito.q: What are Cognito Lambda triggers for?
cognito.a: Custom logic at points in auth flows, such as pre sign-up validation, custom messages or adding claims before token generation.
cognito.simple: Triggers let your own code join in at sign-up or sign-in, like checking details or adding info to a pass.

cognito.q: How do identity pools map users to IAM roles?
cognito.a: In three ways: default roles for authenticated and unauthenticated users, rules that match token claims, or a role taken from the token. Scope the role policies with identity ID variables.
cognito.simple: Identity pools give signed-in and guest users different badges, or pick a badge using details on their pass.

cognito.q: How can one Cognito user pool record which tenant a user belongs to?
cognito.a: With a custom attribute such as custom:tenantID. Make it immutable or read-only to the app client, so users can't change their own tenant. AWS calls this a fit for surface-level tenancy.
cognito.simple: Give each user a tenant label they can't edit themselves, carried in their sign-in token.

cognito.q: When is one shared user pool not enough for multi-tenancy?
cognito.a: When tenants need strong isolation or their own settings, such as per-tenant MFA rules or branding. Then use separate app clients or a user pool for each tenant.
cognito.simple: When each customer needs its own sign-in rules or look, give them their own pool or app client.

kms.a: A service for creating and controlling keys that scramble and unscramble data (encryption). Many AWS services use KMS keys to encrypt your stored data (data at rest), and you decide who can use each key.
kms.simple: Kit the Locksmith makes and guards keys that scramble and unscramble data. You decide who uses each one.

kms.q: Do KMS keys ever leave the service unencrypted?
kms.a: No. The key material stays inside FIPS-validated hardware security modules (HSMs), tamper-resistant key vaults, and never leaves them unencrypted. To use a key, you send KMS a request (an API call).
kms.simple: No. Keys never leave Kit's vault unprotected. To use one, you send the vault a request.

kms.a: Each key you create (a customer managed key) has a monthly fee, and each request to use a key is charged. Keys AWS services create for you (AWS managed keys) have no monthly fee.
kms.simple: Each key you make has a small monthly fee, and each use costs a tiny bit. Keys AWS makes for you don't.

kms.a: Data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is encrypted by a KMS key. Bulk data never goes to KMS, keeping encryption fast and scalable.
kms.simple: Lock your data with a small key, then lock that key with the master key. Big data never visits the vault.

kms.q: Customer managed vs AWS managed vs AWS owned keys?
kms.a: Customer managed: you control policies, rotation and deletion. AWS managed: legacy keys with an aws/ alias, in your account. You can view and audit them, and AWS rotates them yearly. AWS owned: in AWS's account, free, and you can't view them.
kms.simple: Your own keys you fully control. AWS managed keys sit in your account, run by AWS. AWS owned ones stay hidden.

kms.a: The resource policy that controls access to a KMS key. Every key has exactly one. Unless the key policy allows it, IAM policies alone can't give access to the key.
kms.simple: Every key has one key policy: its own rulebook for who may use it. Without it, other permissions can't.

kms.q: What happens when you schedule a KMS key for deletion?
kms.a: It enters a waiting period of 7 to 30 days. During that time the key can't be used, and you can cancel the deletion. Once the key is deleted, data encrypted under it is usually unrecoverable.
kms.simple: It waits 7 to 30 days first, and you can change your mind. Once gone, data locked with it is usually lost.

kms.a: Related keys in different Regions with the same key ID and material, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another without re-encrypting.
kms.simple: Matching keys in different Regions, so data locked in one place can be unlocked in another.

kms.q: Symmetric or asymmetric KMS key: which should you create?
kms.a: Symmetric for data you keep in AWS: services that work with KMS encrypt your data only with symmetric keys. Asymmetric keys are a public and private key pair, for signing or for encryption by people outside AWS who can't call KMS. The private key never leaves KMS unencrypted.
kms.simple: Use the one-secret kind for data in AWS. Use the key-pair kind only for signing or for people outside AWS.

kms.q: What does automatic rotation of a KMS key change?
kms.a: Only the key material used for new encryption, every year by default or on a custom period; you can also rotate on demand. The key's ID and policy stay the same, and KMS still decrypts old data with the old material, so apps need no code changes.
kms.simple: Rotation swaps in a fresh secret inside the same key. Old data still opens, and your app doesn't change.

kms.q: What is a KMS grant, and why do AWS services use them?
kms.a: A grant lets one principal use one KMS key for set operations, without changing key or IAM policies. It can allow but never deny. Services that encrypt your data create a grant for a task, use it and retire it when done, which makes grants good for temporary access.
kms.simple: A grant is a temporary pass to use one key. AWS services take one for a job, then hand it back.

shield.a: A distributed denial of service floods an app with traffic from many sources to exhaust its resources and make it unavailable to real users.
shield.simple: It's when a huge crowd of fake visitors floods your app all at once, so real visitors can't get in.

shield.q: What does AWS Shield Standard cost?
shield.a: Nothing extra. Every AWS customer gets it automatically, and it protects against common DDoS floods at the network and transport layers, the raw traffic below web requests.
shield.simple: It's free! Every AWS customer gets Shield Standard, which blocks common floods automatically.

shield.a: A web application firewall: it checks each web request against rules you set and blocks the bad ones. Examples are SQL injection (database commands hidden in a form) and bad bots.
shield.simple: WAF is a guard that checks each web request against your rules and turns away the sneaky ones.

shield.q: Where can you attach an AWS WAF web ACL?
shield.a: To resources such as CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway REST APIs, AppSync APIs and Cognito user pools.
shield.simple: On the front doors: CloudFront, load balancers, API Gateway, Cognito and a few more.

shield.q: Why start with AWS Managed Rules?
shield.a: They are curated rule groups that AWS maintains for common threats, such as OWASP-style attacks and known bad IPs. You get protection without writing rules.
shield.simple: They're ready-made guard rules that AWS keeps up to date, so you're protected without writing your own.

shield.q: What does a rate-based rule do?
shield.a: Counts requests per client key (such as IP) over a time window and blocks or challenges those above your threshold, limiting floods and scrapers.
shield.simple: It counts how often each visitor knocks. Anyone knocking too often is blocked or asked to prove they're real.

shield.q: Why put CloudFront and Route 53 in front for DDoS resilience?
shield.a: Their globally distributed edge absorbs and filters attacks far from your origin, and they are covered by Shield. Keep the origin locked to CloudFront.
shield.simple: Their worldwide front gates soak up attacks far away from your app, and Shield protects them.

shield.a: Enhanced detection and visibility, plus cost-protection credits. It also gives Shield Response Team access, which needs Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations. It includes the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS rule group, now the default defence against HTTP floods.
shield.simple: Shield Advanced adds better spotting, money back for attack costs, and a team of experts on call.

shield.q: What can an AWS WAF rule do with a request that matches it?
shield.a: Allow it or Block it (by default a 403 Forbidden), which ends the checks. Count it and carry on to the next rules, handy for testing a new rule safely. Or send a CAPTCHA puzzle or a silent Challenge to check it isn't a bot.
shield.simple: A rule can let a request in, turn it away, just count it while you test, or ask 'are you human?'

shield.q: What does the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group catch?
shield.a: At the Common level, bots that say what they are, like scrapers, search engines and automated browsers. The Targeted level adds sophisticated bots that hide, using rate limits, CAPTCHA and background browser challenges. It costs extra.
shield.simple: Bot Control spots robots visiting your site, from honest search engines to sneaky ones posing as people.

guardduty.a: A threat detection service: like Gwen on watch, it keeps reading your AWS logs and activity to spot attacks or anyone doing what they shouldn't. For its foundational sources you install no extra software.
guardduty.simple: Gwen never sleeps: she reads your account's logs and shouts the moment something looks suspicious.

guardduty.q: Which foundational data sources does GuardDuty analyse?
guardduty.a: CloudTrail management events (actions in your account), VPC Flow Logs (network traffic) and Route 53 Resolver DNS query logs (name lookups). GuardDuty reads them directly, without you turning them on.
guardduty.simple: Three diaries: who did what in your account, network traffic, and website name lookups. Nothing to switch on.

guardduty.q: Is there a free trial for GuardDuty?
guardduty.a: Yes, 30 days free in each account and Region. After that you pay for the amount it analyses. Malware Protection for S3 has a free tier instead of a trial.
guardduty.simple: Yes, 30 days free in each account and Region. After that you pay for how much it checks.

guardduty.a: An alert describing a potential security issue with a type, severity and affected resource, e.g. an EC2 instance talking to a known crypto-mining domain.
guardduty.simple: A finding is Gwen's alert: what looks wrong, how serious it is, and which thing it's about.

guardduty.a: Optional add-ons such as S3 Protection, EKS Protection, RDS Protection, Lambda Protection, AI Protection, Runtime Monitoring, and Malware Protection for EC2, S3 and AWS Backup.
guardduty.simple: Optional extra watchers for things like your storage, databases, containers, functions and AI.

guardduty.q: How do you auto-respond to GuardDuty findings?
guardduty.a: Findings are sent to EventBridge. A rule there can trigger Lambda or Step Functions to isolate an instance, revoke keys or notify the team.
guardduty.simple: Send alerts to EventBridge, which can run code to lock things down or tell the team.

guardduty.q: What does Malware Protection for S3 do?
guardduty.a: Scans newly uploaded objects in chosen buckets for malware and can tag results, so downstream processes skip or quarantine infected files.
guardduty.simple: It checks new files in your S3 buckets for nasty software, so infected ones can be set aside.

guardduty.q: How do you run GuardDuty across an organisation?
guardduty.a: The management account designates one delegated admin account, the same in every Region. It sets auto-enable for member accounts and sees their findings.
guardduty.simple: One account becomes the head watcher for everyone, switching it on for every account and seeing all alerts.

guardduty.q: How do you quiet GuardDuty findings you'll never act on?
guardduty.a: Create a suppression rule: a filter that archives matching new findings automatically. They aren't sent to EventBridge, Security Hub or S3, but GuardDuty still keeps them for 90 days. Archived findings don't count toward attack sequences, so keep rules narrow.
guardduty.simple: A suppression rule files away alerts you've decided don't matter, so the real ones stand out.

guardduty.q: What is a GuardDuty attack sequence finding?
guardduty.a: Extended Threat Detection links many events across data sources, resources and time into one finding for a multi-stage attack. Weak signals and earlier findings count, as in stolen credentials then data taken from S3. It's on by default at no extra cost.
guardduty.simple: GuardDuty joins small clues into one story of an attack, so you see the whole plot, not just pieces.

cloudwatch.q: Watching health or recording who did what (CloudWatch vs CloudTrail)?
cloudwatch.a: CloudWatch watches how things are running, with metrics (numbers over time), logs and alarms. CloudTrail is the audit log: it records who did what in your account (each API call), when and from where.
cloudwatch.simple: Watt's clock watches how things are running. CloudTrail is the diary of who did what, and when.

cloudwatch.a: It watches a metric, such as CPU use, and switches from OK to ALARM when the value crosses a threshold you set. It can then act, for example send a message through SNS or scale servers with Auto Scaling.
cloudwatch.simple: An alarm watches a number and rings when it goes too high or low, then can send a message or add servers.

cloudwatch.q: What does CloudTrail Event history show by default?
cloudwatch.a: The last 90 days of management events in a Region, such as who created or deleted a resource, free to view. To keep events longer, create a trail that saves them to S3.
cloudwatch.simple: The last 90 days of who changed what, free to look at. Save it to S3 to keep it longer.

cloudwatch.a: A CloudWatch Logs feature for querying log groups interactively. You can filter, aggregate and visualise logs with its own query language, OpenSearch PPL or SQL. It's charged by data scanned.
cloudwatch.simple: Logs Insights lets you search and sum up your logs with questions, and you pay for how much it reads.

cloudwatch.q: Why set a retention period on log groups?
cloudwatch.a: By default logs are kept indefinitely. Setting retention deletes old logs automatically, controlling storage cost and meeting data policies.
cloudwatch.simple: Logs are kept forever unless you say otherwise. Setting a time limit deletes old ones and saves money.

cloudwatch.q: What does CloudWatch anomaly detection do?
cloudwatch.a: Builds a model of a metric's expected pattern (including daily/weekly cycles) so alarms fire on unusual behaviour rather than a fixed threshold.
cloudwatch.simple: It learns what normal looks like, including daily rhythms, and alerts you when something seems odd.

cloudwatch.q: Why enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation?
cloudwatch.a: CloudTrail creates signed digest files. They let you prove log files weren't modified or deleted after delivery, which matters for audits.
cloudwatch.simple: It adds a seal to your diary files, so you can prove nobody changed or removed them later.

cloudwatch.a: A trail created in the management or delegated admin account that logs events for every account in the organisation to a central location.
cloudwatch.simple: One diary that records what happens in every account in your organisation, in one place.

cloudwatch.q: How do composite alarms cut alarm noise?
cloudwatch.a: A composite alarm watches other alarms and combines their states with AND, OR and NOT. Your team gets one notice when any web server alarm fires, not a flood, or a notice only when the CPU and memory alarms are both in ALARM.
cloudwatch.simple: A composite alarm bundles several alarms into one, so the team gets one clear alert instead of a pile.

cloudwatch.q: What is a CloudWatch Synthetics canary?
cloudwatch.a: A script on a schedule that follows the same routes and actions as a customer, checking your web pages and APIs for availability and latency, with screenshots. You find problems before customers do, even when no one is using the app.
cloudwatch.simple: A canary is a robot visitor that tries your website every few minutes, so you hear about problems first.

securityagent.a: A frontier agent, now part of AWS Continuum, that reviews designs and code for security risks, models threats and runs on-demand penetration tests against your own applications.
securityagent.simple: An AI helper that checks your app's plans, code and running site for ways an attacker could get in.

securityagent.a: An authorised, simulated attack on your own application to find weaknesses before a real attacker does. AWS Security Agent runs multi-step attack chains and confirms each finding by exploiting it.
securityagent.simple: A practice attack on your own app, with permission, to find holes before a real attacker does.

securityagent.q: Which AWS Security Agent features are ready, and which are still in preview?
securityagent.a: On-demand penetration testing is generally available and billed. Design review, code review and threat modelling are still in preview and not billed, within monthly limits per account.
securityagent.simple: Practice attacks are ready and paid for. Design and code reviews are still free previews.

securityagent.q: Why must you verify a domain before a pen test?
securityagent.a: AWS Security Agent only tests domains you have proven you own. You add the TXT record it gives you to the domain's DNS, or expose an HTTP route that returns a validation string. Only then can a test start.
securityagent.simple: So it only ever attacks sites you really own. You prove it by adding a record to your domain.

securityagent.q: What's the difference between target URLs and accessible URLs?
securityagent.a: Target URLs are your verified domains, the ones the agent tests. Accessible URLs are domains it may reach, such as a sign-in provider, but doesn't test. Requests to anything else are blocked by the network.
securityagent.simple: Targets get tested. Accessible sites are only visited, like the sign-in page, and never attacked.

securityagent.q: What are out-of-scope URLs for in a pen test?
securityagent.a: They stop AWS Security Agent from testing those paths. Mark anything destructive or irreversible, such as bulk deletes, payment capture or sending emails, so the test can't cause real harm.
securityagent.simple: They keep the agent away from pages that delete, pay or send messages, so the test can't do real harm.

securityagent.q: How is AWS Security Agent penetration testing priced?
securityagent.a: $50 per task-hour, metered per second. An average test takes about 24 task-hours, roughly $1,200.
securityagent.simple: By the hour the agent works: an average test costs about $1,200.

securityagent.q: What does each AWS Security Agent pen test finding include?
securityagent.a: Proof: the agent confirms the flaw by exploiting it, then reports a CVSS score, reproduction steps and the impact. It can open a pull request with a fix, and retest once you've fixed it.
securityagent.simple: Proof that it's real, how bad it is, how to repeat it, and often a ready-made fix.

securityagent.q: Where can AWS Security Agent's targets be hosted, and where does it run?
securityagent.a: Targets can be on AWS, Azure, GCP or on premises, and private endpoints connect through a VPC. The service itself runs in a limited set of AWS Regions, so check where it's offered first.
securityagent.simple: It can test apps hosted almost anywhere, but the service runs only in some AWS Regions.

securityagent.q: Why should pen tests run against pre-production rather than the live app?
securityagent.a: The agent uses intentionally minimal-impact payloads and guardrails, such as reading a database version instead of dropping a table. Business logic can still react in surprising ways, so AWS recommends testing pre-production.
securityagent.simple: Even a careful practice attack can trip real business rules, so test a copy, not the live app.

bedrock.a: A service for using foundation models, large AI models from Amazon and other AI companies. You call them to build generative AI apps that write text or make images, with no servers to run.
bedrock.simple: Bede the Guide gives you many big AI models in one place, to write text or make pictures, with no servers.

bedrock.q: What is a token in a foundation model?
bedrock.a: A small unit of text, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark, that the model reads or writes. On-demand text models bill per input and output token, so shorter prompts cost less.
bedrock.simple: A token is a small piece of text, like a word or part of one. You pay per token, so shorter asks cost less.

bedrock.q: Is your Bedrock prompt data used to train the base models?
bedrock.a: No. Bedrock doesn't use your prompts or the model's replies (completions) to train AWS or third-party models, and doesn't share them with model providers.
bedrock.simple: No. Your questions and the answers are not used to train the models, or shared with the model makers.

bedrock.q: What do Bedrock Knowledge Bases do?
bedrock.a: Managed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). They ingest your documents, chunk and embed them into a vector store, then retrieve relevant passages to ground model answers with citations.
bedrock.simple: They let the AI look things up in your own documents first, so its answers are grounded and show sources.

bedrock.a: A consistent request format for chatting with any supported model, including tool use, so you can swap models without rewriting code.
bedrock.simple: One common way to chat with any supported model, so you can swap models without rewriting your code.

bedrock.a: Configurable safeguards for inputs and outputs. They include content and prompt-attack filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information masking, contextual grounding and Automated Reasoning checks.
bedrock.simple: Guardrails are safety rails for AI: they block off-limits topics, rude words and private details.

bedrock.q: Why run model evaluations in Bedrock?
bedrock.a: To compare models or prompts on your own dataset, using automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge or human review. Then you choose on evidence, not hype.
bedrock.simple: Test models on your own examples and compare the results, so you pick on evidence, not hype.

bedrock.q: How does prompt caching cut cost and latency?
bedrock.a: It caches a repeated prompt prefix, such as long instructions or documents. Later requests reuse it, so supported models process less input.
bedrock.simple: If the start of your ask is always the same, it's remembered and reused, so it's cheaper and quicker.

bedrock.q: When should you use Bedrock batch inference instead of calling the model directly?
bedrock.a: When you have lots of prompts and don't need the answers right away. Put the prompts in files in S3 and submit one batch job; Bedrock processes them asynchronously and writes the responses back to S3. An EventBridge rule can tell you when it's done.
bedrock.simple: Got thousands of questions and no rush? Drop them in S3 as one job and collect all the answers later.

bedrock.q: Geographic or global cross-Region inference in Bedrock?
bedrock.a: Both let Bedrock pick a Region to run your request, for more throughput, with no extra routing cost and data kept on the AWS network. Geographic profiles stay inside an area such as the US or EU, for data residency rules. Global profiles use any commercial Region and cost about 10% less.
bedrock.simple: Bedrock can send your request to another Region. Keep it in one area for data rules, or go worldwide to save.

agentcore.a: AWS's platform for deploying and running AI agents securely, with no servers for you to manage. It works with any agent framework (the code library an agent is built with) and any AI model.
agentcore.simple: Ace's academy runs AI agents safely for you, with no servers to manage, whatever model or toolkit they use.

agentcore.a: Software that uses a model to reason, plan and take actions with tools to reach a goal, rather than only answering one prompt.
agentcore.simple: An agent is an AI helper that plans and uses tools to reach a goal, not just answer one question.

agentcore.a: A ready-made agent loop: think, use a tool, check the result, repeat. You give it a model, a system prompt (standing instructions) and tools in one API call, and harness runs the loop, the tools and memory for you.
agentcore.simple: A ready-made agent loop: think, use a tool, check, repeat. You give it a model, instructions and tools.

agentcore.q: How does AgentCore Runtime isolate sessions?
agentcore.a: Each user session runs in its own dedicated microVM with isolated compute, memory and filesystem. The microVM is terminated and sanitised when the session ends.
agentcore.simple: Each user's session gets its own tiny private computer, which is wiped clean when the session ends.

agentcore.a: Short-term keeps turn-by-turn context in a session. Long-term extracts insights such as preferences, facts and summaries that persist across sessions.
agentcore.simple: Short-term memory remembers this chat. Long-term memory keeps useful facts and likes for next time.

agentcore.a: Converts APIs, Lambda functions and services into MCP-compatible tools, and connects existing MCP servers. Agents reach them all through one endpoint.
agentcore.simple: Gateway turns your existing tools and services into tools agents can use, all through one doorway.

agentcore.q: What problem does AgentCore Identity solve?
agentcore.a: Agent authentication and access. It works with existing IdPs such as Cognito or Okta, and manages credentials so agents can act securely on users' behalf.
agentcore.simple: It gives agents a proper badge, so they can safely act for users with the right permissions.

agentcore.q: How do Observability and Policy govern agent fleets?
agentcore.a: Observability traces each agent step via OpenTelemetry into CloudWatch. Policy intercepts Gateway tool calls with deterministic, Cedar-compatible rules.
agentcore.simple: Observability records every step an agent takes, and Policy checks each tool call against firm rules.

agentcore.q: What does each AgentCore Runtime session get?
agentcore.a: Its own microVM, with separate compute, memory and filesystem. When the session ends the microVM is terminated and its memory sanitized. By default a session stops after 15 minutes idle or 8 hours in total.
agentcore.simple: Its own tiny private computer, wiped clean when the session ends.

agentcore.q: What can AgentCore Gateway turn into MCP tools?
agentcore.a: Lambda functions, OpenAPI specs, Smithy models and API Gateway REST API stages, and it can connect existing MCP servers. Outbound auth to each target can use an API key, OAuth or IAM.
agentcore.simple: Your functions and web APIs, so an agent can find and call them as tools.

agentcore.q: Where does AgentCore support the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol?
agentcore.a: In AgentCore Runtime: with serverProtocol set to A2A, the container serves JSON-RPC on port 9000 and an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json. AWS says broader A2A support across other AgentCore services is coming.
agentcore.simple: In Runtime, so the agents you host there can talk to other agents in a shared language.

sagemaker.a: A service for making your own machine learning (ML) models, programs that learn patterns from data. You write code in notebooks, train the model on AWS servers, then host it so apps can use it.
sagemaker.simple: Sage's workshop is where you build your own AI models: gather data, then train, test and share them.

sagemaker.q: Why does machine learning (ML) need training data?
sagemaker.a: A model learns patterns from examples. Its quality depends on having enough relevant, correctly labelled data that reflects real use.
sagemaker.simple: A model learns from examples, so it's only as good as its data: enough of it, labelled right, like real life.

sagemaker.q: How is SageMaker AI training billed?
sagemaker.a: You pay per second of training for each server (instance) you use, at that instance type's rate, with no upfront fees. Billing stops when the job ends, unless you keep a warm pool (servers kept ready for the next job).
sagemaker.simple: You pay per second for the computers used while training, and the bill stops when the job ends.

sagemaker.q: What is a SageMaker training job?
sagemaker.a: A managed run that reads data, usually from S3, and trains on the instances you choose. It uses a built-in algorithm, your script or your container, then saves the model to S3.
sagemaker.simple: A training job reads your data, teaches the model on the computers you pick, then saves the finished model.

sagemaker.q: How can you cut SageMaker training cost?
sagemaker.a: Use Managed Spot Training, which runs on spare EC2 capacity at a discount. Add checkpoints to S3 so interrupted jobs resume instead of restarting.
sagemaker.simple: Train on spare computers at a discount, and save progress often so an interrupted job can pick up again.

sagemaker.q: Which inference options does SageMaker AI offer?
sagemaker.a: Real-time endpoints, serverless inference, asynchronous inference for large or slow requests, and batch transform for offline datasets.
sagemaker.simple: Your model can answer right away, only when called, slowly for big jobs, or for a whole pile at once.

sagemaker.q: How does a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint handle changing traffic?
sagemaker.a: With an auto scaling policy you attach, it adds instances as traffic rises and removes them as it falls, between the minimum and maximum you set.
sagemaker.simple: Add a scaling rule and it adds computers as traffic rises and removes them as it falls.

sagemaker.q: How do Pipelines and Model Registry enable MLOps?
sagemaker.a: Pipelines automate data prep, training and evaluation steps. The Model Registry versions models with an approval status that gates deployments.
sagemaker.simple: Pipelines run the steps for you, and the registry keeps each model's versions and whether it's approved.

sagemaker.q: What does SageMaker JumpStart give you?
sagemaker.a: Pretrained, open-source models for many kinds of problems, which you can fine-tune, evaluate and deploy from SageMaker Studio or the Python SDK, plus solution templates and example notebooks. Check each third-party model's licence before you use it.
sagemaker.simple: JumpStart is a shelf of ready-made models you can tune on your data and launch, instead of starting from zero.

sagemaker.q: When does a SageMaker multi-model endpoint save money?
sagemaker.a: When you host many models that use the same ML framework, some rarely called. They share one fleet and serving container, and SageMaker AI loads models into memory as traffic needs. Expect cold-start delays for rarely used models; give busy, latency-critical ones their own endpoint.
sagemaker.simple: Many similar models can share one set of servers. Cheaper, but a rarely used model may answer slowly at first.

q.a: AWS's AI assistants. Q Developer helps you build on AWS, and Kiro is now the successor to its plugins for code editors (IDEs). Q Business answers from company data but is closed to new customers, and its successor is Amazon Quick.
q.simple: Amazon Q is AWS's family of AI helpers, like Quill, who answers questions as you work on AWS.

q.a: A managed assistant that answers questions from enterprise data. It's now closed to new customers, and AWS points them to its successor, Amazon Quick.
q.simple: Q Business answers questions from a company's own information. It's closed to new customers now.

q.q: Where can you use Q Developer besides the code editor (IDE)?
q.a: In the AWS Management Console (AWS's website for managing your account), the console mobile app, AWS docs, and chat apps like Slack and Teams. In the console it explains your resources, costs and errors.
q.simple: Right in the AWS website, the mobile app, the docs and team chat apps, where it explains your stuff and costs.

q.q: What happens to Q Developer IDE plugins?
q.a: New sign-ups stopped on May 15, 2026, and the IDE plugins and paid subscriptions lose support on April 30, 2027. Kiro is the successor. Q in the console and chat apps continues.
q.simple: They're being retired: new sign-ups stopped in 2026, and Kiro takes over. Q in the console keeps going.

q.q: What does the 'Diagnose with Amazon Q' button in the AWS console do?
q.a: It appears on supported console errors, such as missing permissions or a hit service limit. Amazon Q explains the error, then gives you steps to fix it.
q.simple: When the console shows an error, that button asks Q to explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

q.q: When Amazon Q answers questions about your AWS resources, what can it see?
q.a: Only what your own IAM permissions allow. It calls get, list and describe APIs for you, and it can't read the data inside resources, such as objects in an S3 bucket.
q.simple: Only what your own permissions let you see. It can list your things, but can't open the files inside them.

q.q: What can Amazon Quick, the successor to Amazon Q Business, do?
q.a: It's an AI assistant for work that answers from your company's connected documents and apps. It can also build dashboards, run in-depth research and automate tasks.
q.simple: Amazon Quick is a work helper that answers from your company's documents and apps, and can automate tasks.

q.q: How can an admin let users chat with Amazon Q but stop it calling AWS APIs for them?
q.a: Deny the q:PassRequest action, which Q needs to act on your behalf. To block only some services, deny them with the aws:CalledVia condition set to q.amazonaws.com.
q.simple: Take away the one permission Q needs to act for you, so it can still chat but can't change anything.

q.q: What can you ask Amazon Q Developer about your AWS bill?
q.a: Past and forecast costs from Cost Explorer, savings ideas from Cost Optimization Hub and Compute Optimizer, Savings Plans options and service prices, in your own words. It answers from your account's real data and shows which APIs it called.
q.simple: Ask Q 'why did my bill go up?' in plain words. It checks your real costs and shows where it found the answer.

q.q: What does Amazon Q Developer in chat applications (formerly AWS Chatbot) do?
q.a: It forwards AWS notifications from SNS topics, such as CloudWatch alarms with charts, to Slack, Microsoft Teams or Amazon Chime channels, so a team can respond together. You can ask Amazon Q questions and run AWS CLI commands from the channel.
q.simple: It posts AWS alerts into your team chat, where you can ask Q questions and fix things together.

rekognition.a: A computer vision service: it looks at your images and videos and tells you what's in them. It can find objects, scenes, text, faces and unsafe content.
rekognition.simple: Rex looks at your pictures and videos and tells you what's in them: things, places, words and faces.

rekognition.a: Labels such as 'Car' or 'Beach', each with a confidence score (how sure it is). Some also get a bounding box showing where the object is, and apps use them to tag and search images automatically.
rekognition.simple: Labels like 'Car' or 'Beach', each with a score for how sure it is, and sometimes a box showing where.

rekognition.q: How is Rekognition image analysis priced?
rekognition.a: You pay per image processed, or per minute for stored video, with no upfront commitment. Volume tiers lower the price.
rekognition.simple: You pay for each picture checked, or each minute of video, and the more you use, the cheaper it gets.

rekognition.q: How does Rekognition read images from S3?
rekognition.a: Pass an S3Object (bucket + key) and Rekognition reads it directly. The bucket must be in the same Region, and the caller needs read access.
rekognition.simple: Just tell Rex the bucket and file name in S3, and he reads the picture straight from there.

rekognition.a: DetectModerationLabels returns labels for unsafe or inappropriate content with confidence, so you can flag, blur or route items to human review.
rekognition.simple: It spots unsafe or rude pictures and says how sure it is, so you can hide them or ask a person to check.

rekognition.a: Start an async job, such as StartLabelDetection, on a video in S3. Rekognition notifies an SNS topic when it completes, then you fetch the results.
rekognition.simple: Start a job on a video in S3. Rex rings a bell when he's done, and then you collect the results.

rekognition.q: Does a face collection store the face images?
rekognition.a: No. It stores face feature vectors extracted from images, not the images themselves, for search and comparison.
rekognition.simple: No. It stores a number pattern of each face's features, not the pictures themselves.

rekognition.a: When built-in labels miss your domain, e.g. your own product parts. Train a model on your labelled images to detect them.
rekognition.simple: When the usual labels don't know your things, like your own parts. Teach it with your own labelled pictures.

rekognition.q: What does Rekognition Face Liveness check?
rekognition.a: That the person verifying their identity is really in front of the camera, not someone spoofing their face with a photo or video, or an attack that bypasses the camera. The user takes a short video selfie and gets a confidence score from 0 to 100.
rekognition.simple: Face Liveness checks a real, live person is at the camera, not a photo or a video of someone else.

rekognition.q: Can Rekognition tell if workers wear protective equipment?
rekognition.a: Yes. DetectProtectiveEquipment finds face covers, hand covers and head covers on people in an image, predicts whether each covers the right body part, and returns bounding boxes for the people and items.
rekognition.simple: Yes. It can spot masks, gloves and helmets in a photo and say if they're worn properly.

textract.a: A machine learning service that reads scanned documents. It pulls out printed and handwritten text, plus tables and form data, going beyond simple OCR (plain text recognition).
textract.simple: Tex reads scanned pages and copies out the printed and handwritten words, tables and forms for you.

textract.a: OCR, optical character recognition, turns a picture of text into text a computer can search and edit. Textract also works out the structure, such as which text is a table cell or a form answer.
textract.simple: Character recognition turns a picture of words into text you can search. Textract also spots tables and forms.

textract.a: Per page processed. The price depends on which features you use: reading plain text costs less than tables, forms or queries (questions you ask about the page).
textract.simple: You pay per page, and plain reading costs less than finding tables, forms or answers to questions.

textract.q: What does AnalyzeDocument add over DetectDocumentText?
textract.a: Feature types such as TABLES, FORMS (key-value pairs), QUERIES, SIGNATURES and LAYOUT, returning structured relationships between blocks.
textract.simple: The fuller reader also finds tables, form answers, signatures and layout, and how they fit together.

textract.a: Ask natural language questions like 'What is the policy number?' and get the answer extracted, without knowing the document layout.
textract.simple: Ask a page a question like 'What's the policy number?' and Tex finds the answer for you.

textract.q: How do you process multi-page PDFs?
textract.a: Use asynchronous operations, such as StartDocumentAnalysis, on documents in S3. Textract publishes completion to SNS, then you page through the results.
textract.simple: For long documents, start a background job on the file in S3, then collect the pages when it's done.

textract.a: AnalyzeExpense for invoices and receipts, AnalyzeID for US government IDs, and Analyze Lending for mortgage packages. Analyze Lending runs async only, via StartLendingAnalysis.
textract.simple: Special readers for receipts and invoices, American identity cards, and big home loan document bundles.

textract.q: How do you add human review to Textract results?
textract.a: Every result carries a Confidence score, so send low scores to a review step. Amazon A2I did this for AnalyzeDocument but no longer takes new customers.
textract.simple: Every answer comes with a score for how sure it is. Send unsure ones to a person to check.

textract.q: What does Textract's Layout feature add?
textract.a: It labels the parts of a page: title, headers and footers, section titles, page numbers, lists, figures, tables, key-value pairs and paragraph text, each with a bounding box. Elements come back in reading order, column by column, so text from multi-column pages stays in order.
textract.simple: Layout says which text is a title, a heading or a paragraph, and returns it in the order people read it.

textract.q: What is a Textract adapter, and when would you train one?
textract.a: An adapter customises Textract for your own kind of document. You annotate sample documents, train the adapter, review its accuracy, then pass it to AnalyzeDocument with your queries. Retrain it later to improve it further.
textract.simple: If Textract misreads your special forms, teach it with your own examples so it gets them right.

apprunner.a: A service that deploys a web app straight from your source code or a container image, then runs, load-balances and scales it for you, with no servers or load balancer to set up. Since 30 April 2026 it takes no new customers; existing customers keep using it.
apprunner.simple: Hand Remy your code and he runs it as a website. New teams now use ECS Express Mode instead.

apprunner.q: Can a new AWS customer start using App Runner today?
apprunner.a: No. AWS closed App Runner to new customers. Existing customers can keep using it as normal, even creating new services, and AWS keeps investing in its security and availability, but plans no new features. For new apps AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode.
apprunner.simple: No. Teams already on it can stay, but new teams are sent to ECS Express Mode.

apprunner.q: Where can App Runner deploy an app from?
apprunner.a: From a container image in a registry such as Amazon ECR, or from source code in a GitHub or Bitbucket repository. For code, a managed runtime (Python, Node.js, Java and others) builds the container image for you, with no Dockerfile to write.
apprunner.simple: From a ready container image, or straight from code in a repository that App Runner builds for you.

apprunner.q: What do App Runner auto scaling settings control?
apprunner.a: Max concurrency (how many requests one instance handles before App Runner adds another), max size (the most instances) and min size (instances always provisioned). You pay for the memory of every provisioned instance, but for CPU only on the ones actively serving.
apprunner.simple: How busy each copy may get, and the fewest and most copies. Idle copies cost only their memory.

apprunner.a: Per second for the vCPU and memory of instances while they handle requests, plus memory for provisioned instances while they wait. Automatic deployments add a set monthly fee per app, and builds from source code are billed by build time.
apprunner.simple: You pay for computer time while it works, a little memory while it waits, and extra for builds.

apprunner.q: What web address does a new App Runner service get?
apprunner.a: A subdomain of awsapprunner.com, served over HTTPS. You can link up to five custom domains; with Route 53 as your DNS provider, the console adds the certificate validation and DNS records for you.
apprunner.simple: A ready web address with a padlock. You can add up to five of your own names too.

apprunner.q: How does an App Runner service reach a database in a private subnet?
apprunner.a: Through a VPC connector: choose private subnets (ideally in three Availability Zones) and security groups, and all outgoing traffic goes through your VPC. Incoming traffic still arrives at the public domain. Reaching the internet or AWS APIs then needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints.
apprunner.simple: A private side door lets the app call your database. Visitors still come in the front.

apprunner.q: When does App Runner deploy a new version by itself?
apprunner.a: With the automatic deployment trigger on, App Runner builds and deploys each time you push a commit to the source directory, or push a new image version to the image repository.
apprunner.simple: Every time you push new code or a new image, Remy picks it up and runs the new version.

apprunner.q: How do you move an App Runner service to ECS Express Mode with no downtime?
apprunner.a: Create an Express Mode service from the same container image, add your custom domain and certificate to its load balancer, then shift traffic with Route 53 weighted records (10, 25, 50, 75, then 100 percent). Keep App Runner running 24 to 48 hours so a rollback is just a weight change.
apprunner.simple: Run the new copy beside the old one, move visitors over bit by bit, and keep the old one to switch back.

apprunner.q: What does ECS Express Mode build from one API call?
apprunner.a: From a container image and two IAM roles (a task execution role and an infrastructure role) it creates an ECS service on Fargate, an Application Load Balancer, auto scaling and networking in your own account. Express Mode adds no charge; you pay for the resources it creates.
apprunner.simple: Give it a container and two roles, and it builds the whole website setup in your account.

apprunner.q: An App Runner app deploys from source code. What changes when it moves to Express Mode?
apprunner.a: Express Mode deploys container images only, so add a build step first: a Dockerfile, a push to a registry such as Amazon ECR, then the deploy. A pipeline such as GitHub Actions can rebuild and deploy on each push, as App Runner did.
apprunner.simple: Package the code as a container first. A pipeline can then rebuild and redeploy it on each push.

batch.a: A fully managed service for batch computing at any scale. You submit containerised jobs; Batch provisions the compute, schedules the jobs and scales capacity to the work queued, with no batch software to install or manage.
batch.simple: Bram bakes big piles of jobs for you: he lights just enough ovens, then lets them cool.

batch.a: No. There is no additional charge for AWS Batch. You pay for the compute it starts to run your jobs, such as EC2 instances or Fargate.
batch.simple: Batch itself is free. You pay for the ovens it lights: the servers or containers your jobs use.

batch.q: What are the four building blocks of AWS Batch?
batch.a: Jobs (the units of work, run as containers), job definitions (the blueprint: image, CPU, memory, role), job queues (where submitted jobs wait) and compute environments (the managed or unmanaged capacity jobs run on).
batch.simple: Jobs are orders, job definitions are recipes, queues are the order rail, and compute environments are ovens.

batch.q: What is an array job in AWS Batch?
batch.a: One submission that fans out into 2 to 10,000 child jobs sharing the same job definition. Each child reads its own index from the AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX variable: ideal for Monte Carlo simulations, parameter sweeps or rendering.
batch.simple: One order slip for thousands of batches: each oven gets its own number and bakes its own part.

batch.q: Which compute can a managed Batch compute environment use?
batch.a: Fargate, Amazon EC2 (On-Demand or Spot Instances) or Amazon ECS Managed Instances. You set the instance types and the minimum, desired and maximum vCPUs, and Batch launches and stops capacity to fit the jobs queued.
batch.simple: Rented ovens of different kinds. Bram starts more when orders pile up and stops them when done.

batch.q: What does RUNNABLE mean for a Batch job?
batch.a: The job has no outstanding dependencies and waits for enough resources in one of its queue's compute environments. It starts as soon as capacity fits, but can stay RUNNABLE indefinitely if none ever does, a common thing to troubleshoot.
batch.simple: The order is ready to bake and waits for a free oven big enough.

batch.q: How do you cut Batch costs with Spot Instances?
batch.a: Use a Spot compute environment with the SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED allocation strategy, which picks the Spot pools least likely to be interrupted at the lowest price, and give jobs a retry strategy so an interrupted job runs again.
batch.simple: Rent spare ovens cheaply, pick the ones least likely to be taken back, and rebake any cut-off batch.

batch.q: How do automated retries work in AWS Batch?
batch.a: A retry strategy gives a job 1 to 10 attempts; a failed attempt puts it back in RUNNABLE. With evaluateOnExit (up to 6 rules) you can retry only for certain reasons, such as a host failure, and exit for the rest. Cancelled or terminated jobs are not retried.
batch.simple: Bram can rebake a failed batch up to ten times, and only for the failures worth retrying.

batch.q: How do you start a Batch job when a file arrives in S3, or on a schedule?
batch.a: Make the job queue the target of an EventBridge rule. A rule can submit a job for each matching event, such as an object upload, with the input transformer passing the bucket and key as job parameters. For schedules, AWS recommends EventBridge Scheduler.
batch.simple: A bell rings when a file arrives or the clock strikes, and a new order lands on Bram's rail.

batch.q: What is fair-share scheduling in AWS Batch?
batch.a: By default a job queue runs jobs first in, first out, so urgent work can get stuck behind earlier jobs. Attaching a scheduling policy turns on fair-share scheduling: share identifiers divide the queue's compute between users or workloads.
batch.simple: Instead of strict first come, first served, each team gets its fair share of the ovens.

batch.q: What are multi-node parallel jobs in AWS Batch?
batch.a: Single jobs that span several EC2 instances (gang scheduling), for large high-performance computing or distributed GPU training with frameworks such as MPI. The main node starts first, then the child nodes; the job finishes when the main node exits.
batch.simple: One giant cake baked across many ovens at once, all started together and led by a head oven.

lightsail.a: The easiest way to start on AWS for websites and web apps. It bundles virtual private servers (instances), container services, managed databases, load balancers, a content delivery network, SSD storage, static IP addresses and DNS management for a low, predictable monthly price.
lightsail.simple: Skye rents you a ready-rigged server for one monthly price, with storage and data included.

lightsail.q: What does a Lightsail instance plan include?
lightsail.a: Memory, vCPUs, SSD storage and a data transfer allowance in one monthly price; only outbound data beyond the allowance costs extra. For example, the smallest Linux plan with a public IPv4 address is $5 a month: 512 MB of memory, 2 vCPUs, 20 GB of SSD and 1 TB of transfer.
lightsail.simple: One price covers the computer, its disk and lots of data. Only data beyond that costs extra.

lightsail.q: What can a Lightsail instance start from?
lightsail.a: An image (blueprint) with a plain operating system, a development stack such as LAMP or Node.js, or a ready application such as WordPress, Drupal or Magento, so you skip installing the software yourself.
lightsail.simple: A ready-made starting kit: a bare system, a coding setup, or an app like WordPress already installed.

lightsail.q: Why attach a static IP to a Lightsail instance?
lightsail.a: An instance's default public IP address changes every time you stop and start it. A static IP stays the same, so your domain's DNS records keep working. It costs nothing while attached to an instance, but is charged when it isn't attached.
lightsail.simple: So the address doesn't change when you restart. It's free while it's in use.

lightsail.q: How does a Lightsail instance firewall work?
lightsail.a: Each instance has an IPv4 and an IPv6 firewall made of allow rules: a protocol, a port and the source addresses. They filter traffic arriving at the public IP; all outbound traffic is allowed. Limit SSH and RDP to your own IP address.
lightsail.simple: You list which doors are open and who may knock. Keep the admin door open only to you.

lightsail.q: What do Lightsail automatic snapshots keep?
lightsail.a: Once turned on, Lightsail takes a daily snapshot of the instance or disk and keeps the latest seven. They are deleted with the instance, so copy one to a manual snapshot to keep it. Windows instances and managed databases don't support automatic snapshots.
lightsail.simple: A copy every day, the last seven kept. Save one by hand if you want to keep it for good.

lightsail.q: How does a Lightsail load balancer keep a site up?
lightsail.a: It spreads web traffic across Lightsail instances in several Availability Zones, health-checks them and sends requests only to healthy ones. Attach a validated Lightsail certificate for HTTPS. The instances should share a central database and media storage.
lightsail.simple: One gate sends visitors to healthy servers in different zones, so one failing server doesn't stop the site.

lightsail.q: What managed databases does Lightsail offer?
lightsail.a: MySQL or PostgreSQL plans with memory, processing, storage and a transfer allowance included, in standard or high availability configurations, for a fixed monthly price. They scale separately from your instances.
lightsail.simple: Ready-run databases for a fixed monthly price, kept apart from your servers so each can grow.

lightsail.q: How do you move a Lightsail instance to Amazon EC2?
lightsail.a: Export an instance snapshot to EC2. It becomes an AMI and an EBS snapshot (plus one more EBS snapshot per attached disk) in the same Region, from which you launch an EC2 instance. For another Region, copy the snapshot there in Lightsail first.
lightsail.simple: Export a snapshot and it becomes an EC2 starting image, ready to launch a bigger server.

lightsail.q: When should you choose Amazon EC2 instead of Lightsail?
lightsail.a: When you need advanced networking, flexible pay-per-use or commitment pricing, hundreds of instance types, or close integration with services such as RDS, DynamoDB or Lambda. Lightsail fits simple sites, small apps and prototypes with fixed, predictable costs.
lightsail.simple: When you outgrow simple: special networks, many server types, or tight links to other AWS services.

lightsail.q: How can a Lightsail project use other AWS services?
lightsail.a: Lightsail keeps a focused set of features, but you can connect your project to other AWS services through Amazon VPC peering, so your instances can reach resources such as databases in your account's VPC.
lightsail.simple: A private link lets your Lightsail servers talk to the rest of your AWS account.

backup.a: A fully managed service that centralises and automates data protection across AWS services, in the cloud and on premises. You set backup policies once and monitor backups of many resource types in one place, instead of service by service with custom scripts.
backup.simple: Bea backs up the whole city's data on a timetable, all from one office.

backup.a: Many resource types, including EC2 instances, EBS volumes, S3 data, DynamoDB tables, RDS and Aurora databases, EFS and FSx file systems, DocumentDB, Neptune and Redshift clusters, EKS clusters, CloudFormation stacks and Storage Gateway volumes.
backup.simple: Disks, files, buckets, tables and databases from many AWS services, all from one place.

backup.q: What are a backup plan, a backup vault and a recovery point?
backup.a: A backup plan says when and how to back up and how long to keep each copy. A backup vault is the container that stores and encrypts the backups. Each backup the plan makes is a recovery point you can restore.
backup.simple: The plan is the timetable, the vault is the strongroom, and each saved copy is one you can restore.

backup.q: How do you assign resources to a backup plan?
backup.a: By resource ID, or by tags: every resource with the tag you choose, for example backup=daily, is backed up under the plan, so one plan covers many services consistently.
backup.simple: Stick a label on what matters, and everything with that label gets backed up.

backup.q: How long can AWS Backup keep backups?
backup.a: Snapshot backups from 1 day to 100 years, or indefinitely. Continuous backups for point-in-time restore keep 1 to 35 days. Supported backups can move to cheaper cold storage, where they must then stay at least 90 days.
backup.simple: Snapshots for a day up to a hundred years; second-by-second backups for up to 35 days.

backup.q: Why are AWS Backup backups incremental?
backup.a: For supported resource types, the first backup is a full copy and each later one stores only what changed, so you can back up often while storing less. Resource types without incremental support make a full copy each time.
backup.simple: Bea copies everything once, then only what changed, so backing up often stays cheap.

backup.q: How do you protect backups from losing a whole Region or account?
backup.a: Add a copy rule to the plan: each backup is copied to a vault in another Region, or to another account in your AWS Organizations organization. You can fan backups in to one central account, then fan them out again for resilience.
backup.simple: Send a copy of every backup to a far-away vault, in another Region or another account.

backup.q: Governance mode or compliance mode for Vault Lock?
backup.a: Governance mode can be removed by users with enough IAM permissions. Compliance mode becomes immutable after a grace time of at least 72 hours: from then on no one, not the root user and not AWS, can delete backups early or change the lock.
backup.simple: Trusted admins can open a governance lock. Once set, nobody can open a compliance lock.

backup.q: What does AWS Backup restore testing do?
backup.a: On a schedule it restores the latest or a random recovery point of chosen resources, times the restore, optionally lets you validate the result, then deletes the restored resources. It proves backups really restore, and the results help show compliance.
backup.simple: Every so often Bea restores a backup for real, times it, checks it, then tidies up.

backup.q: What is a logically air-gapped vault?
backup.a: A special backup vault with extra protection: it is always locked in compliance mode, encrypted with an AWS owned key by default (or your own KMS key), and you can share access with other accounts so they can restore quickly after an incident.
backup.simple: An extra-sealed vault, always locked, that another account can use to restore fast.

backup.q: How do you manage backups across many AWS accounts?
backup.a: Use backup policies through AWS Organizations, so backup plans apply automatically to the accounts in your organization. AWS Backup Audit Manager then checks backups against controls you choose and reports daily on compliance.
backup.simple: Write the backup rules once for the whole company, and a daily report shows who follows them.

kinesis.q: What is Amazon Kinesis Data Streams?
kinesis.a: A service that collects and processes streams of data records in real time, such as logs, website clicks or market feeds. A record is typically ready to read less than a second after it is written, and several applications can read the same stream.
kinesis.simple: Kenzie's millrace: live data rushes in, in order, and many wheels can read it at once.

kinesis.q: What is a shard in a Kinesis data stream?
kinesis.a: A sequence of records with a fixed capacity: up to 1 MB or 1,000 records per second written, and 2 MB per second read. A stream is one or more shards, and its capacity is the sum of theirs.
kinesis.simple: One lane of the river. More lanes carry more water.

kinesis.q: How long does a Kinesis data stream keep records?
kinesis.a: 24 hours by default. You can raise retention up to 8,760 hours (365 days); retention over 24 hours costs extra. Until a record expires, any application can read it again.
kinesis.simple: A day by default, up to a year for a little more, and readers can go back and read again.

kinesis.q: What does a record's partition key do?
kinesis.a: Kinesis hashes it to pick the shard, so records with the same key land on the same shard, in order. Choose a key with many values, such as a user id, so records spread evenly across shards.
kinesis.simple: A label on each record: same label, same lane, kept in order.

kinesis.q: On-demand or provisioned capacity for a Kinesis stream?
kinesis.a: On-demand needs no capacity planning: it scales on its own, ready for up to double the peak write throughput of the last 30 days, and you pay per GB. Provisioned means you choose the number of shards, billed per shard-hour, which suits predictable traffic.
kinesis.simple: Let the river widen by itself and pay per use, or dig a set number of lanes yourself.

kinesis.q: How does Lambda read a Kinesis data stream?
kinesis.a: An event source mapping reads each shard and invokes your function with batches of records, one batch per shard at a time, in order. A parallelization factor of up to 10 runs more batches per shard at once while keeping order per partition key.
kinesis.simple: Lambda takes scoops of records from each lane, in order, and can take several scoops at once when busy.

kinesis.a: A consumer that gets its own 2 MB per second from each shard, pushed to it over HTTP/2 with about 70 ms delay, instead of sharing one 2 MB per second with every other reader. A stream can have up to 20 of them (50 with On-demand Advantage).
kinesis.simple: Each reader gets its own private pipe from every lane instead of sharing one.

kinesis.q: What happens when a Lambda function keeps failing on a Kinesis batch?
kinesis.a: By default Lambda retries until the records expire, so one bad record can block its shard for up to a week. Set a maximum retry count and record age, bisect failed batches to isolate the bad record, and send failures to an on-failure destination.
kinesis.simple: One broken record can jam a lane. Limit retries, split the batch, and set the bad record aside.

kinesis.q: How do you encrypt the records in a Kinesis stream?
kinesis.a: Turn on server-side encryption: Kinesis encrypts records with an AWS KMS key as producers put them in. Producers and consumers then need permission to use that key, and the KMS calls are billed.
kinesis.simple: Turn on encryption with a key, and every record is scrambled as it enters the river.

kinesis.q: When is a Kinesis stream a better fit than an SQS queue?
kinesis.a: When several applications must each read the same records, in order per key, and may need to read them again later. A stream keeps every record for its retention period; a queue hands each message to one consumer, which deletes it once processed.
kinesis.simple: When many readers need every record, in order, and may need to rewind. A queue gives each job to one worker.

kinesis.q: How many shards does a provisioned stream need?
kinesis.a: The larger of (write KB per second / 1,024) and (read KB per second / 2,048), rounded up, where read bandwidth is write bandwidth times the number of consumers. Change the count with UpdateShardCount as traffic grows.
kinesis.simple: Count how much flows in and how many readers there are, then dig enough lanes for the bigger need.

opensearch.a: A managed service that deploys, runs and scales OpenSearch clusters in the AWS Cloud. OpenSearch is an open-source search and analytics engine for log analytics, real-time app monitoring and clickstream analysis.
opensearch.simple: Ola's tower runs a search engine for you: fast searches through text, logs and clicks, with no servers to run.

opensearch.q: What is an OpenSearch Service domain?
opensearch.a: A domain is an OpenSearch cluster: the settings, instance types, instance counts and storage you choose. Each instance in it is one node, and OpenSearch Service replaces failed nodes for you.
opensearch.simple: A domain is your own search cluster. Each machine in it is a node, and broken ones are swapped out for you.

opensearch.a: An on-demand option with no clusters to size. You create a collection (a group of indexes) for search, time series or vector search, and capacity scales up and back down with use.
opensearch.simple: No machines to pick: you make a collection, and it grows and shrinks with how much you search.

opensearch.q: How many primary shards does OpenSearch Service give a new index by default?
opensearch.a: Five primary shards, each with one replica: 10 shards in all. Open-source OpenSearch defaults to one of each. Primary shards are hard to change later, so decide before you index the first document.
opensearch.simple: Five main pieces, plus a copy of each. Choose the count before you start: changing it later is hard.

opensearch.q: How big should each shard be?
