opensearch.a: Roughly 10–30 GiB where search speed matters most, and 30–50 GiB for write-heavy work such as log analytics. Very large shards slow recovery, and too many small ones waste CPU and memory.
opensearch.simple: Not too big, not too small: about 10 to 50 GiB each, at the smaller end when quick searches matter most.

opensearch.q: What does Multi-AZ with Standby give an OpenSearch Service domain?
opensearch.a: The domain spans three AZs, each holding a full copy of the data, and one zone's nodes wait as standby. If infrastructure fails, standby takes over in under a minute, for 99.99% availability at no extra cost.
opensearch.simple: Three zones each hold all the data, one on standby. If a zone fails, standby takes over in under a minute.

opensearch.q: Why put an OpenSearch Service domain in a VPC?
opensearch.a: A VPC domain has no public endpoint: only resources that can reach the VPC can call it, and traffic stays within the AWS Cloud. You choose VPC or public access when you create the domain and can't switch later.
opensearch.simple: In your private network, nobody on the internet can reach it. Decide at the start: you can't switch later.

opensearch.a: Cheaper storage for read-only data you query less often, such as older logs. UltraWarm nodes keep data in Amazon S3 with caching, at a much lower cost per GiB than hot storage on the data nodes.
opensearch.simple: Older logs you rarely read move to a cheaper back room backed by S3, and you can still search them.

opensearch.q: How can a DynamoDB table's items become searchable in OpenSearch without custom code?
opensearch.a: Use the zero-ETL integration. An OpenSearch Ingestion pipeline loads a snapshot through DynamoDB export to S3, then follows DynamoDB Streams to copy changes in near real time, using none of the table's throughput.
opensearch.simple: A ready-made pipeline copies the table, then keeps up with every change, without slowing the table down.

opensearch.q: How does OpenSearch help a GenAI app find meaning, not just matching words?
opensearch.a: With vector search. You store embeddings and find the nearest neighbours by distance or similarity (k-NN). Vector search collections in OpenSearch Serverless can be the vector store for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
opensearch.simple: It stores number fingerprints of meaning, so an AI can find passages that say the same thing in other words.

opensearch.q: What does fine-grained access control add to an OpenSearch Service domain?
opensearch.a: Permissions inside the data: at the index, document and field level, mapped to users and roles, so each person sees only the indexes, documents and fields they're allowed to.
opensearch.simple: Each person sees only their own shelves, pages or even single lines of the index.

documentdb.a: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) is a fully managed document database. You can run the same application code, drivers and tools that you use with MongoDB.
documentdb.simple: Doc's archive keeps data as whole folders, and apps written for MongoDB can talk to it unchanged.

documentdb.a: A NoSQL database that stores and queries data as JSON-like documents. A document can nest objects inside objects, and documents can each have different fields.
documentdb.simple: Each record is a folder that can hold folders inside, and no two folders need the same shape.

documentdb.q: When is a document database a good fit?
documentdb.a: When the schema must stay flexible for fast, changing development: user profiles where each user shares different details, content management, and real-time data from many sources.
documentdb.simple: When records differ a lot, like user profiles, and your app keeps changing what it stores.

documentdb.q: How does DocumentDB keep its storage durable?
documentdb.a: Storage and compute are separate. The cluster volume keeps six copies of your data across three AZs, and it grows by itself in 10 GB steps as you add data.
documentdb.simple: Six copies across three zones, and the storage grows by itself as you add more.

documentdb.q: How many replica instances can a DocumentDB cluster have?
documentdb.a: Up to 15. Replicas share the cluster's storage, so they don't repeat writes; they serve reads, and if the primary fails DocumentDB fails over to a replica in another AZ.
documentdb.simple: Up to 15 helpers answer reads, and one takes over if the main machine fails.

documentdb.a: By default, yes: encryption in transit is turned on for new clusters, so clients must connect over TLS. It's set by the tls parameter in the cluster parameter group.
documentdb.simple: Yes, by default: apps must use a locked, encrypted line to talk to it.

documentdb.q: Can you restore DocumentDB to an exact moment?
documentdb.a: Yes. Automated backups give point-in-time recovery to any second in the retention period, up to the last 5 minutes. Retention can be set up to 35 days.
documentdb.simple: Yes: rewind to any second in the last 35 days, up to about five minutes ago.

documentdb.q: How can code react when data in DocumentDB changes?
documentdb.a: Turn on change streams and use the cluster as a Lambda event source. Lambda invokes your function each time data changes, for instance-based clusters (not elastic or global clusters).
documentdb.simple: A running list of every change lets a function wake up each time a folder is updated.

documentdb.q: What do DocumentDB elastic clusters add?
documentdb.a: Elastic clusters handle millions of reads and writes per second and petabytes of storage, without you choosing, managing or upgrading instances.
documentdb.simple: A version that spreads across many machines for huge sizes, with no machines for you to pick.

documentdb.q: What does a DocumentDB global cluster do?
documentdb.a: One primary Region takes writes and copies them to up to 10 read-only secondary Regions, usually in under a second. In a Region-wide outage you can promote a secondary, typically in under a minute.
documentdb.simple: Read-only copies in up to 10 other Regions. If one Region goes down, another can take over in about a minute.

documentdb.q: Can DocumentDB do vector search for GenAI apps?
documentdb.a: Yes, on DocumentDB 5.0 instance-based clusters. You store embeddings beside your JSON documents and search for the most similar ones, for semantic search, recommendations and chatbots.
documentdb.simple: Yes: it can find documents that mean something similar, right beside the data your app already keeps.

transitgateway.a: A network transit hub that connects your VPCs and on-premises networks. It acts as a Regional virtual router: each network attaches to it once, instead of being linked to every other network.
transitgateway.simple: Tess's interchange: every network drives in once and can reach the others, instead of a road to each.

transitgateway.q: Why use a hub instead of peering every VPC with every other?
transitgateway.a: VPC peering isn't transitive: if A peers with B and with C, B still can't reach C through A. Linking every pair grows fast, while a hub needs one attachment per VPC.
transitgateway.simple: Peering only links pairs, so many networks need lots of links. A hub needs one link for each network.

transitgateway.q: What can you attach to a transit gateway?
transitgateway.a: VPCs, Site-to-Site VPN connections, Direct Connect gateways, Transit Gateway Connect attachments for SD-WAN appliances, and peering connections to other transit gateways.
transitgateway.simple: Your private networks, your office's links, and other hubs in other Regions or accounts.

transitgateway.q: How does a VPC attachment reach each Availability Zone?
transitgateway.a: You pick exactly one subnet in each AZ you enable, and the transit gateway puts a network interface there. Resources can only reach it from AZs where it has an attachment, so enable several.
transitgateway.simple: Give it one small room in each zone. Zones without one can't use the hub, so set it up in several.

transitgateway.q: What decides where traffic goes inside a transit gateway?
transitgateway.a: Transit gateway route tables. Each attachment is associated with exactly one route table, and its routes (static or propagated) pick the next attachment by destination IP address.
transitgateway.simple: Its route tables: each network follows one table, which says which exit leads to each address.

transitgateway.q: Do you need two transit gateways for high availability?
transitgateway.a: No. Transit gateways are highly available by design. For redundancy, AWS recommends a single transit gateway in each Region.
transitgateway.simple: No. One hub per Region is already built to keep running; you don't need a spare.

transitgateway.q: What do you pay for with Transit Gateway?
transitgateway.a: An hourly charge for each attachment, plus the amount of traffic the transit gateway processes. By default, data processing is charged to the account that owns the source attachment.
transitgateway.simple: Each network plugged in costs a little every hour, plus a charge for the traffic that passes through.

transitgateway.q: How can test VPCs be kept apart from production on one transit gateway?
transitgateway.a: Associate test VPCs with one route table and production VPCs with another. An attachment only reaches what its route table has routes for, like separate routers inside one hub.
transitgateway.simple: Give test and live networks different route tables, so they share a hub but can't reach each other.

transitgateway.q: How do other AWS accounts attach to your transit gateway?
transitgateway.a: Share it with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), and the other accounts' owners can attach their VPCs. AWS suggests keeping it in a central network services account.
transitgateway.simple: Share it with your other accounts, and they can plug their own networks into the same hub.

transitgateway.q: How do you see what traffic crosses a transit gateway?
transitgateway.a: Turn on Transit Gateway Flow Logs. They record IP traffic to and from the transit gateway and publish it to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Firehose, without affecting throughput or latency.
transitgateway.simple: Flow logs note every trip through the hub and send the list to CloudWatch or S3 to read later.

transitgateway.q: How do transit gateways in different Regions connect?
transitgateway.a: With a peering attachment: the other side accepts it, then you add static routes that point at it. Traffic between Regions is encrypted and travels on the AWS network.
transitgateway.simple: Hubs in different Regions shake hands, then routes send traffic across, encrypted on AWS's own network.

globalaccelerator.a: A service that improves availability and performance for local and global users. It gives your app static IP addresses and carries users' traffic over the AWS global network to your endpoints.
globalaccelerator.simple: Axel's express line: visitors board at the nearest stop and ride AWS's own network to your app.

globalaccelerator.q: How many static IP addresses does an accelerator get?
globalaccelerator.a: Two static IPv4 addresses, or four with dual-stack (two IPv4 and two IPv6). They're anycast from the AWS edge network and stay assigned as long as the accelerator exists.
globalaccelerator.simple: Two fixed addresses, answered from many places at once, that stay yours while the accelerator exists.

globalaccelerator.q: How does Global Accelerator shorten the trip to your app?
globalaccelerator.a: Traffic enters at the edge location closest to the user, then travels the well-monitored, congestion-free AWS global network, so it spends less time on the public internet.
globalaccelerator.simple: Users get on at the closest stop, then skip the busy public roads for AWS's quieter private ones.

globalaccelerator.q: What endpoints can a standard accelerator send traffic to?
globalaccelerator.a: Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, EC2 instances and Elastic IP addresses, in one AWS Region or several.
globalaccelerator.simple: Load balancers, servers or fixed server addresses, in one Region or many.

globalaccelerator.q: What happens when an endpoint becomes unhealthy?
globalaccelerator.a: A standard accelerator health-checks every endpoint, and sends new connections to another healthy endpoint as soon as one fails.
globalaccelerator.simple: It checks every stop all the time, and sends new riders to a healthy one as soon as one breaks.

globalaccelerator.q: How is Global Accelerator different from CloudFront?
globalaccelerator.a: Both use AWS edge locations. CloudFront speeds up cacheable and dynamic web content. Global Accelerator proxies TCP or UDP traffic to apps in one or more Regions: good for gaming, IoT and voice, or apps that need static IP addresses or fast Region failover.
globalaccelerator.simple: CloudFront keeps copies of web content near people. Axel carries any kind of traffic quickly to your app.

globalaccelerator.q: Why is its failover quicker than changing DNS records?
globalaccelerator.a: Some devices and resolvers cache DNS answers for a long time. Global Accelerator's IP addresses never change, so a change takes effect in seconds, with no wait for caches to expire.
globalaccelerator.simple: Old addresses can linger in phones and browsers. Axel's addresses never change, so switching takes seconds.

globalaccelerator.q: What are traffic dials and endpoint weights?
globalaccelerator.a: A traffic dial sets what share of traffic an endpoint group in a Region gets, for example during tests or upgrades. Endpoint weights split traffic between endpoints inside a group.
globalaccelerator.simple: Dials choose how much traffic each Region gets; weights split it between servers inside that Region.

globalaccelerator.q: How does Global Accelerator help protect your app?
globalaccelerator.a: Your origins hide behind two static entry points that AWS Shield protects from DDoS attacks by default. It can reach internal load balancers and private EC2 instances, keeping them off the public internet.
globalaccelerator.simple: Visitors only see Axel's two addresses, which are shielded from floods, and your servers can stay private.

globalaccelerator.q: What is a custom routing accelerator for?
globalaccelerator.a: Sending each user to a specific EC2 instance and port in a VPC subnet, chosen by your own logic, such as putting players in one game session or callers on one media server.
globalaccelerator.simple: Your app picks the exact server for each user, like seating game players at the same table.

globalaccelerator.q: Can you use your own IP addresses with Global Accelerator?
globalaccelerator.a: Yes. Bring your own IPv4 address range (BYOIP) and use it for the accelerator's static entry points, so apps with hard-coded addresses can move to AWS without client changes.
globalaccelerator.simple: Yes: bring your own fixed addresses, so customers' apps and firewalls need no change.

secretsmanager.a: A service that stores, hands out and rotates secrets such as database passwords, API keys and OAuth tokens. Your code asks for a secret when it runs, so the secret never has to sit in the source code.
secretsmanager.simple: Sid keeps passwords and API keys in a strongroom and hands them to your code only when it runs.

secretsmanager.q: Why shouldn't a password be written into the code?
secretsmanager.a: Anyone who can read the code, or the app built from it, can read the password, and changing it means redeploying. With Secrets Manager the code fetches the secret at run time; rotate the old one so the leaked copy stops working.
secretsmanager.simple: Anyone who sees the code sees the password. Fetch it from Sid at run time and change the old one.

secretsmanager.a: You pay per secret per month and per 10,000 API calls ($0.40 a secret a month and $0.05 per 10,000 calls in AWS's examples). Secrets marked for deletion are free, and Lambda rotation functions bill at Lambda's rate.
secretsmanager.simple: A small monthly fee for each secret and a tiny fee for calls. Secrets waiting to be deleted are free.

secretsmanager.q: What does rotating a secret do?
secretsmanager.a: It updates the credential in both the secret and the database or service, on a schedule you set, as often as every four hours. Apps that fetch the secret each time get the new value without being redeployed.
secretsmanager.simple: Rotation changes the password in the database and in the strongroom together. Apps just keep asking Sid.

secretsmanager.q: Managed rotation or rotation by a Lambda function?
secretsmanager.a: Managed rotation is run by the service that owns the secret, such as RDS, Aurora, DocumentDB or Redshift for their admin passwords, with no Lambda function. Other secrets rotate with a Lambda function that Secrets Manager calls step by step.
secretsmanager.simple: Some services change their own passwords for you. For everything else, a small function does it.

secretsmanager.a: With envelope encryption: KMS makes a data key that encrypts the secret value, and a KMS key encrypts that data key. You choose the free AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager or a symmetric customer managed key.
secretsmanager.simple: Every secret is locked with a key from Kit's vault: AWS's free one or one you manage yourself.

secretsmanager.q: What are the AWSCURRENT, AWSPENDING and AWSPREVIOUS labels?
secretsmanager.a: Staging labels on a secret's versions. AWSCURRENT is the version returned by default, AWSPENDING is the new value while rotation runs, and AWSPREVIOUS is the one before, so you can roll back.
secretsmanager.simple: Name tags on a secret's versions: the one in use now, the one being made, and the one before.

secretsmanager.a: Single user changes one user's password and suits most cases, but calls with the old password may be denied for a moment, so retry. Alternating users keeps two users and changes them in turn, so apps always get valid credentials.
secretsmanager.simple: One user is simplest. Two users taking turns means the app always has a password that works.

secretsmanager.q: How do you let a role in another AWS account read a secret?
secretsmanager.a: Attach a resource-based policy to the secret naming that role. Secrets Manager checks new policies with automated reasoning (Zelkova) to stop you granting broad access, and BlockPublicPolicy refuses public ones.
secretsmanager.simple: Give the secret its own rulebook naming who may read it. Sid refuses rules that open it to everyone.

secretsmanager.q: How do replica secrets help an app that runs in several Regions?
secretsmanager.a: Secrets Manager copies the encrypted secret, its tags and resource policy to the Regions you pick, each encrypted with a KMS key there. Rotate the primary and the new value reaches every replica; a replica can be promoted to standalone.
secretsmanager.simple: Copies of the secret wait in other Regions. Change the main one and every copy updates too.

secretsmanager.q: What happens when you delete a secret?
secretsmanager.a: It stops working at once but is kept for a recovery window of at least seven days, free, and you can restore it. A CloudWatch alarm on access attempts shows if an app still uses it. Replicas must be deleted first.
secretsmanager.simple: Sid locks it away for at least a week first, so you can change your mind if something still needs it.

inspector.a: A vulnerability management service. It finds your EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR and Lambda functions by itself, and keeps scanning them for known software flaws and unintended network exposure.
inspector.simple: Ingrid checks your servers, container images and functions for known flaws, and keeps checking.

inspector.a: A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry: a public ID for a known security flaw in software. Inspector reports packages exposed to CVEs, which attackers can exploit while they stay unpatched.
inspector.simple: A public reference number for a known flaw in a piece of software. Ingrid tells you which you have.

inspector.a: Per resource scanned: EC2 instances by the average number assessed in a month, container images per scan and rescan, and Lambda functions per month. New accounts get a 15-day free trial.
inspector.simple: You pay for each server, image and function it checks. New accounts try it free for 15 days.

inspector.q: When does Inspector scan a resource again?
inspector.a: Automatically, whenever something changes that could add a flaw: a new package installed on an instance, a patch, or a newly published CVE that affects it. There are no scan schedules to set up.
inspector.simple: Whenever something changes: new software, a patch, or news of a fresh flaw. No timetable needed.

inspector.q: Agent-based or agentless scanning of EC2 instances?
inspector.a: Agent-based scanning collects the software list through the SSM Agent on the instance; agentless scanning reads it from EBS snapshots. New accounts start in hybrid mode, which uses both.
inspector.simple: Ingrid either asks a helper on the server or looks at a copy of its disk. By default she does both.

inspector.a: A severity score tailored to your environment. Inspector starts from the CVSS base score in the National Vulnerability Database and adjusts it, for example lowering it when a flaw needs the network but the instance has no open path to the internet.
inspector.simple: Ingrid's own danger rating for your setup. A flaw nobody can reach from the internet scores lower.

inspector.q: Which kinds of finding does Inspector raise?
inspector.a: Package vulnerability (software exposed to a CVE), code vulnerability (lines of code that can be exploited, from Lambda code scanning and Code Security) and network reachability (an open network path to an instance).
inspector.simple: Three kinds: risky software packages, risky lines of code, and doors left open to the network.

inspector.q: How do you act on Inspector findings automatically?
inspector.a: Inspector sends each finding to EventBridge as an event, where a rule can run a Lambda function or notify through SNS. Findings also go to Security Hub. Once you fix the problem, Inspector notices and closes the finding.
inspector.simple: Each finding goes to EventBridge, which can run code or tell the team. Fixed problems close themselves.

inspector.q: What does Lambda code scanning add to standard scanning?
inspector.a: Standard scanning checks a function's packages and layers for CVEs. Code scanning also checks your own code for flaws such as data leaks, injection and weak cryptography. Functions encrypted with customer managed keys aren't scanned.
inspector.simple: Standard checks the parts you borrowed. Code scanning also reads the code you wrote yourself.

inspector.q: How do you run Inspector across an organization?
inspector.a: Through AWS Organizations, make one account the delegated administrator. It can activate Inspector for every account in one click, auto-activate new members and see all their findings in one place.
inspector.simple: One account switches Ingrid on for every account and sees all their findings together.

macie.a: A data security service that finds sensitive data in your S3 buckets using machine learning and pattern matching, and keeps checking the buckets' security and access settings.
macie.simple: Mae checks your S3 buckets for personal or secret data and spots buckets left open.

macie.q: What counts as sensitive data for Macie?
macie.a: Credentials such as private keys and AWS secret access keys; financial information such as credit card and bank account numbers; and personal information such as passport, driver's licence and health insurance numbers.
macie.simple: Passwords and keys, card and bank numbers, and personal details like passport numbers.

macie.q: Is there a free trial for Macie?
macie.a: Yes, 30 days the first time you enable it. The trial covers checking your buckets' security and access, and can include automated sensitive data discovery, but not discovery jobs.
macie.simple: Yes, 30 days free to check your buckets. Deep searches you start yourself aren't included.

macie.q: Policy findings or sensitive data findings?
macie.a: A policy finding reports a possible security or privacy problem with a bucket, such as it becoming public. A sensitive data finding reports sensitive data Macie found inside an object.
macie.simple: One kind says a bucket is badly set up. The other says a file holds sensitive data.

macie.q: Automated discovery or a discovery job?
macie.a: Automated sensitive data discovery keeps sampling representative objects across all your buckets, for a broad view. A sensitive data discovery job is a deeper, targeted analysis of buckets you choose, run once or on a schedule.
macie.simple: Automatic checks sample every bucket a little. A job searches the buckets you pick, in depth.

macie.q: What is a custom data identifier?
macie.a: Your own rule for sensitive data: a regular expression for the text pattern, plus optional keywords and a proximity rule. Use it for data only your organization has, which the managed identifiers don't know.
macie.simple: Your own pattern for secret data only your company has, like its own reference numbers.

macie.q: What is an allow list in Macie?
macie.a: Text or text patterns Macie should ignore in objects, such as your organization's public phone numbers or sample test data, so they don't raise sensitive data findings.
macie.simple: A list of things Mae should ignore, like your shop's public phone number.

macie.q: How do you act on Macie findings automatically?
macie.a: Macie publishes findings to EventBridge as events, where rules can run a Lambda function or notify through SNS. It can also publish findings to Security Hub.
macie.simple: Findings go to EventBridge, which can run code or alert the team, and on to Security Hub.

macie.q: Can Macie show you the sensitive data it found?
macie.a: Yes, if you set it up: it can retrieve and reveal samples, the first 1 to 10 occurrences of each type, up to 128 characters each, encrypted with a KMS key you specify.
macie.simple: Yes, if you allow it: Mae can show a few short samples, locked with your own key.

macie.q: How do you run Macie across many accounts?
macie.a: Integrate it with AWS Organizations (or use invitations). A Macie administrator account can enable Macie for members, review their buckets and policy findings, and look for sensitive data in their buckets.
macie.simple: One account switches Mae on for all the others and checks all their buckets.

securityhub.a: A unified cloud security service. It gathers signals from posture checks, Inspector (software flaws), Macie (sensitive data) and GuardDuty (threats), correlates them and ranks the critical issues so you can respond at scale.
securityhub.simple: Hana puts every security warning on one board and ranks the worst first.

securityhub.q: What are Security Hub's best-practice checks?
securityhub.a: Security Hub CSPM (cloud security posture management) runs checks, called controls, against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS and PCI DSS. Each failed check becomes a control finding.
securityhub.simple: Hana checks your setup against lists of good habits, like keeping buckets private, and flags misses.

securityhub.q: Can you try Security Hub's best-practice checks for free?
securityhub.a: Yes. The first time you enable Security Hub CSPM in an account, it gets a 30-day free trial. You still pay for other services it uses, such as AWS Config items, but not for Config rules turned on only by its standards.
securityhub.simple: Yes, 30 days free in each account. Other services it leans on may still cost a little.

securityhub.q: What is a security standard in Security Hub CSPM?
securityhub.a: A set of requirements based on regulations, industry best practice or company policy. Enabling a standard turns on all its controls, and Security Hub checks them and produces findings. You can turn single controls off.
securityhub.simple: A checklist of good habits. Switch one on and Hana starts checking every item on it.

securityhub.a: A score from 0 to 100 percent for each enabled standard, based on how its controls are doing; the summary score averages them. It needs AWS Config resource recording and updates every 24 hours.
securityhub.simple: A percentage of passed checks for each checklist, updated once a day.

securityhub.q: Why does Security Hub CSPM need AWS Config?
securityhub.a: Most controls are checked with service-linked AWS Config rules, so you must enable AWS Config and record your resources for Security Hub CSPM to produce most control findings.
securityhub.simple: Most of Hana's checks read the city's records in AWS Config, so Config has to be switched on.

securityhub.q: Which format are Security Hub findings in?
securityhub.a: Security Hub generates and receives findings in the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF), including those from GuardDuty, Macie and Inspector. Security Hub CSPM uses the AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF).
securityhub.simple: Every warning is written the same way, whichever watcher raised it, so they're easy to compare.

securityhub.a: Rules, made in the administrator account, that update findings as they arrive: for example raise a finding to CRITICAL when it's about a business-critical resource, or suppress INFORMATIONAL ones. They apply to new and updated findings.
securityhub.simple: Rules that sort warnings as they arrive, like marking anything about the payments server urgent.

securityhub.a: You choose a home Region (once called the aggregation Region) and link others. Findings, insights, control statuses and security scores from the linked Regions all appear in the home Region, so you manage them in one place.
securityhub.simple: Pick one Region as home, and warnings from your other Regions show up there too.

securityhub.a: Security Hub correlates findings from Security Hub CSPM checks, Inspector and other services to detect exposures of one resource. An attack path graph shows how an attacker could reach and take control of it.
securityhub.simple: Hana joins small clues about one resource into one warning, with a map of how an attacker could get in.

securityhub.q: What does Security Hub's unused access analysis find?
securityhub.a: IAM roles, users, access keys and permissions not used in the last 90 days. It creates a service-linked IAM Access Analyzer, and for unused permissions it can suggest a smaller replacement policy.
securityhub.simple: Badges and keys nobody has used for 90 days, with a smaller set of permissions to swap in.

polly.a: A service that turns text into lifelike speech, in many languages and voices. You pay only for the text you convert, and you can cache and replay the audio at no extra cost.
polly.simple: Pip reads your text aloud in a natural voice. Save the audio and play it again for free.

polly.a: Four: generative (the most human-like and conversational), long-form (for long content such as articles and training), neural (high quality) and standard. You pick an engine and a voice for each request.
polly.simple: Four kinds of voice, from plain to very human, including one for long stories.

polly.a: Per character of text converted, billed monthly. The rate depends on the engine: standard is cheapest, then neural, generative and long-form. Each engine has a monthly free allowance to start with.
polly.simple: You pay for each letter Pip reads, and plainer voices cost less. There's a free allowance each month.

polly.a: Speech Synthesis Markup Language: tags around your text, inside <speak>, that control how Polly says it, such as pauses, speed, pitch, volume, emphasis and pronunciation.
polly.simple: Little tags in the text that tell Pip to pause, slow down, speak louder or say a word a certain way.

polly.a: A list, in the W3C Pronunciation Lexicon Specification format, that tells Polly how to say particular words, for example reading 'W3C' as 'World Wide Web Consortium'. Lexicons are stored per Region.
polly.simple: A word list telling Pip how to say tricky words, like names or short forms.

polly.q: Which audio formats can Polly return?
polly.a: MP3 or Ogg Vorbis for web and mobile apps, or PCM for devices and telephony. It can also return speech marks instead of audio.
polly.simple: Common sound files for apps and websites, or raw sound for phone systems.

polly.a: No. Polly speaks text in the language it's written in, and numbers written as digits are read in the voice's language. Translate the text first if you need another language.
polly.simple: No. Pip reads text in the language it's written in. Translate it first if you need another.

polly.a: Metadata about the speech, such as where each sentence and word starts and ends in the audio. Use them to highlight words as they're read or to sync a character's lips in an animation.
polly.simple: Timings for each word, so an app can highlight words as Pip says them or move a character's lips.

polly.q: How do you turn a long article into audio?
polly.a: SynthesizeSpeech handles up to 3,000 billed characters in near real time. For longer text, StartSpeechSynthesisTask works in the background on up to 100,000 billed characters, saves the file to S3 and can notify an SNS topic.
polly.simple: Short text comes back straight away. Long text is done in the background and saved to S3.

polly.q: Why might a generative voice sound slightly different months later?
polly.a: Generative and long-form voices are generative AI models, so updates to the model or its training data can change how a voice sounds a little. That matters for content made over a long time, like a podcast season.
polly.simple: Pip's most human voices can change slightly when they're improved, so a long series may not match.

comprehend.a: A natural language processing (NLP) service that finds insights in text: the entities named, key phrases, language, sentiment and personal data. Its models are pre-trained, so you don't need training data.
comprehend.simple: Nora reads text and tells you who and what it mentions, its language and its mood.

comprehend.q: What does sentiment analysis tell you?
comprehend.a: The main feeling of a text: positive, negative, neutral or mixed, with a score for how likely each is. Use it to see how customers feel about a product from their comments.
comprehend.simple: Whether a comment sounds happy, unhappy, neutral or mixed, and how sure Nora is.

comprehend.a: Most features bill per unit of 100 characters, with a minimum of 3 units a request. The free tier covers 50,000 units (5 million characters) a month per feature for 12 months. Custom models also pay for training and endpoints.
comprehend.simple: You pay per 100 letters read. For a year, the first 5 million letters a month are free for each check.

comprehend.q: What is an entity in Comprehend?
comprehend.a: A reference in the text to a real-world thing, such as a person, location, organization, date, quantity or title, each with a confidence score you can filter on.
comprehend.simple: A name or thing in the text, like a person, a place, a date or an amount.

comprehend.a: Sentiment gives one overall feeling per document. Targeted sentiment gives the feeling about each entity mentioned: in 'The tacos were delicious and the staff was friendly', both tacos and staff are positive.
comprehend.simple: One gives the whole review's mood. The other gives the mood about each thing it mentions.

comprehend.q: How does Comprehend handle personally identifiable information (PII)?
comprehend.a: It finds PII such as addresses, bank account numbers and phone numbers in English or Spanish text, in real time or in a batch job. Redacting it needs an asynchronous batch job.
comprehend.simple: Nora spots personal details like addresses and phone numbers, and can black them out.

comprehend.a: Synchronous calls analyse one document, or up to 25 at once, and answer straight away, for interactive apps. For large sets, put the documents in S3 and start an asynchronous job; the results land in S3.
comprehend.simple: One or a few texts get answers straight away. Big piles go in S3 and are read as a background job.

comprehend.a: You train a classifier on your own labelled examples to sort documents into your own categories, such as routing support requests to the right team. Classify one document in real time, or a set in a job.
comprehend.simple: Teach Nora your own labels with examples, like which team should answer each support message.

comprehend.a: A separate service that finds medical information, such as conditions, medications and protected health information, in clinical text like doctors' notes. It reads US English only and is priced separately.
comprehend.simple: A sister service that reads doctors' notes and finds illnesses and medicines.

comprehend.q: What does a real-time custom model cost while it's idle?
comprehend.a: A custom model used in real time runs on an endpoint, which you pay for from the moment it starts until you delete it, whether or not requests arrive. Use auto scaling, and delete endpoints you no longer need.
comprehend.simple: A live custom model costs money every hour it's switched on, so turn it off when you're done.

comprehend.q: How do you keep the text Comprehend reads private?
comprehend.a: Encrypt the input in S3, and use your own KMS key to encrypt job output and the storage volume of the instance that runs the job. IAM controls who may call Comprehend.
comprehend.simple: Lock the input, the results and the working disk with your own key, and let only chosen roles in.

stepfunctions.a: Stef's service for workflows, also called state machines. Each step is a state, and Step Functions runs them in order, calling Lambda or other AWS services for the work, so you write less glue code.
stepfunctions.simple: Stef runs the steps of a job in order, calling other services for each one, so you write less glue code.

stepfunctions.q: What are a state and an execution?
stepfunctions.a: A state is one step in a workflow, such as a Task state that asks another AWS service to do some work. An execution is one run of the workflow, from its first state to its last.
stepfunctions.simple: A state is one step. An execution is one run of the whole workflow, start to finish.

stepfunctions.a: Standard workflows are billed per state transition, retries included, and 4,000 transitions a month are free with no end date. Express workflows are billed per request, by duration and by memory used.
stepfunctions.simple: Standard workflows pay per step, with 4,000 free each month. Express ones pay per run and its length.

stepfunctions.q: What does a Choice state do?
stepfunctions.a: It adds if-then logic: it checks the state's input against its rules and picks the next state. Give it a Default, because if no rule matches and there's no Default, the execution fails.
stepfunctions.simple: A Choice state is a fork in the road: it looks at the data and picks which step comes next.

stepfunctions.q: What is the difference between a Parallel state and a Map state?
stepfunctions.a: Parallel runs different branches at the same time and waits for all of them to finish; if one fails, the whole state fails. Map runs the same steps once for each item in a list, with the iterations in parallel.
stepfunctions.simple: Parallel plays different parts at once. Map plays the same part once for every item in a list.

stepfunctions.q: How do Retry and Catch handle a failed step?
stepfunctions.a: By default an error fails the whole execution. Retry tries the step again, 3 times by default, waiting twice as long each time. Catch sends an error that keeps happening to a fallback state instead.
stepfunctions.simple: Retry tries a failed step again, waiting a bit longer each time. Catch sends the error to a backup step.

stepfunctions.q: What is the Amazon States Language?
stepfunctions.a: The JSON-based language a workflow is written in. It names the states, says which one starts, and links each state to the next. The console shows the same workflow as a diagram.
stepfunctions.simple: The way a workflow is written down: a list of steps and which one comes next. The console draws it.

stepfunctions.q: Standard or Express: which workflow type fits which job?
stepfunctions.a: Standard runs for up to a year, each step exactly once, with full history: good for payments and long jobs. Express runs for up to five minutes at very high rates: good for streaming data. You can't change the type later.
stepfunctions.simple: Standard is for long, careful jobs that must run once. Express is for lots of quick jobs, up to five minutes.

stepfunctions.q: How can a workflow wait for a person to approve something?
stepfunctions.a: Use the wait-for-callback pattern (.waitForTaskToken). The task sends out a task token, for example in a queue message, and the workflow pauses until something returns it with SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. Standard workflows can wait up to a year.
stepfunctions.simple: Stef hands out a ticket and waits. When the person approves and hands it back, the music carries on.

stepfunctions.q: How can Step Functions call AWS services without a Lambda function?
stepfunctions.a: Through service integrations. AWS SDK integrations call the API actions of over two hundred services directly, and optimized integrations add extras for services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS and ECS, like waiting for a job to finish (.sync).
stepfunctions.simple: Stef can call many AWS services herself, so you don't need a function just to pass a message on.

stepfunctions.q: What is a Distributed Map state?
stepfunctions.a: A Map state in Distributed mode runs each item as a child workflow execution with its own history, up to 10,000 at once. It can read a large dataset straight from S3, such as a CSV file or a list of objects.
stepfunctions.simple: For huge jobs, Stef splits the list and runs up to 10,000 small workflows at the same time.

stepfunctions.q: Why do Express workflows suit only work that is safe to repeat?
stepfunctions.a: Asynchronous Express workflows run at least once, so a step might run twice. That suits idempotent work, like writing the same item to DynamoDB again. Payments belong in Standard, which runs each step exactly once unless you add Retry.
stepfunctions.simple: Quick Express jobs might run a step twice. Use them for safe-to-repeat work and Standard for payments.

cloudformation.a: Forma's service for infrastructure as code. You describe the AWS resources you want in a template, and CloudFormation creates and configures them for you, working out what depends on what.
cloudformation.simple: Describe what you want in one file, and CloudFormation builds it all for you, in the right order.

cloudformation.q: What is the difference between a template and a stack?
cloudformation.a: A template is a YAML or JSON text file that describes resources. A stack is what CloudFormation builds from it: you create, update and delete all of its resources together, as one unit.
cloudformation.simple: The template is the blueprint. The stack is the building made from it, looked after as one piece.

cloudformation.a: Nothing extra for resources in the AWS:: namespaces: you pay only for what it creates, like EC2 servers, just as if you'd made them by hand. Third-party resource types and custom hooks are charged per handler operation.
cloudformation.simple: Building AWS resources with CloudFormation is free. You pay only for the resources themselves.

cloudformation.q: Which section must every template have?
cloudformation.a: Resources. Each resource has a logical ID, a type such as AWS::S3::Bucket, and its properties. Parameters, Outputs, Mappings, Conditions and the other sections are optional.
cloudformation.simple: Every blueprint needs a list of Resources. Everything else in it is optional.

cloudformation.q: What are Parameters and Outputs for?
cloudformation.a: Parameters let you pass in values, like an instance type, when you create or update a stack, so one template fits many uses. Outputs hand back values after the build, like a website address, for people or other stacks.
cloudformation.simple: Parameters are the blanks you fill in before building. Outputs are the notes handed back after.

cloudformation.q: What do intrinsic functions such as Ref and Fn::GetAtt do?
cloudformation.a: They fill in values that only exist when the stack runs, such as the name of a bucket created moments earlier. Ref returns a resource's or parameter's value, Fn::GetAtt reads one of a resource's attributes, and Fn::Sub builds text.
cloudformation.simple: They let one part of the blueprint point at another, like 'the bucket I just made'.

cloudformation.q: What happens if a stack fails partway through?
cloudformation.a: CloudFormation rolls back: it undoes the changes so the stack returns to its last stable state. You can choose instead to preserve the resources that succeeded, fix the problem and carry on from there.
cloudformation.simple: If a build fails, Forma takes the half-built parts down again, unless you ask her to keep them.

cloudformation.q: Why preview an update with a change set?
cloudformation.a: A change set lists what an update will do before it happens. Some edits replace a resource: renaming an RDS database instance creates a new database and deletes the old one, losing its data unless you backed it up.
cloudformation.simple: A change set shows what will change before you build. Some small edits quietly replace a whole database.

cloudformation.q: What is drift, and how do you find it?
cloudformation.a: Drift is when someone changes a stack's resource outside CloudFormation, for example in the EC2 console, so it no longer matches the template. Drift detection compares each resource's real settings with the template and lists the differences.
cloudformation.simple: Drift is when someone changes things by hand. Drift detection shows what no longer matches the blueprint.

cloudformation.q: How do you keep a bucket when its stack is deleted?
cloudformation.a: Give it DeletionPolicy: Retain. With no policy, CloudFormation deletes the resource along with the stack. For resources that support snapshots, such as EBS volumes, Snapshot saves one before deleting.
cloudformation.simple: Mark it Retain and it stays when the stack goes. Snapshot saves a copy before it goes.

cloudformation.a: They create, update or delete stacks across many accounts and Regions in one operation, from one template. With AWS Organizations, they can deploy automatically to each new account added to a target OU.
cloudformation.simple: One blueprint, built in every account and Region at once, and in each new account as it joins.

cloudformation.q: How does the AWS CDK relate to CloudFormation?
cloudformation.a: The AWS CDK lets you define infrastructure in a programming language such as TypeScript or Python, from reusable pieces called constructs. It turns your code into CloudFormation templates and deploys them as stacks, with rollback on error.
cloudformation.simple: A coding kit lets you write the blueprint in TypeScript or Python. CloudFormation then builds it.

systemsmanager.a: Manny's depot for looking after servers, called nodes, at scale: in AWS, on premises and in other clouds. From one place you can see them, patch them, run commands and connect, without logging in to each one.
systemsmanager.simple: Manny looks after all your servers from one place: he checks them, patches them and fixes them.

systemsmanager.q: What makes a server a managed node?
systemsmanager.a: The SSM Agent is installed on it and can talk to the Systems Manager service. The agent takes requests from Systems Manager, runs them on the machine and reports back how they went.
systemsmanager.simple: A small helper program, the SSM Agent, runs on the server and does Manny's jobs there.

systemsmanager.a: Many tools cost nothing extra: Run Command on EC2 and standard Parameter Store parameters, for example. Some features are paid, such as advanced parameters, OpsCenter items and just-in-time node access.
systemsmanager.simple: Many of Manny's tools are free for EC2 servers. A few extras cost a little.

systemsmanager.q: How does Session Manager let you in without SSH?
systemsmanager.a: It opens a shell on a managed node from the browser or the AWS CLI, with no inbound ports, no bastion hosts and no SSH keys. IAM policies decide who may connect, and sessions can be logged.
systemsmanager.simple: Manny opens the door from inside, so no door to the street stays open and no keys get lost.

systemsmanager.a: Running the same admin task on many managed nodes at once, such as installing software or collecting log files, without logging in to any of them. It costs nothing extra on EC2 nodes.
systemsmanager.simple: One command, run on every server at once, with no logging in.

systemsmanager.a: Named configuration values, like an endpoint address or an AMI ID, as String, StringList or SecureString (encrypted with KMS). Apps read them at run time instead of hard-coding them. For secrets that need rotating, AWS recommends Secrets Manager.
systemsmanager.simple: A labelled cupboard of settings your apps read when they start, instead of baking them into code.

systemsmanager.q: Standard or advanced parameters: what is the difference?
systemsmanager.a: Standard is the default and costs nothing extra: up to 10,000 parameters per account and Region, 4 KB each. Advanced allows 100,000 parameters, 8 KB values, parameter policies and sharing with other accounts, for a charge, and can't be downgraded.
systemsmanager.simple: Standard settings are free and small. Advanced ones hold more and can be shared, for a fee.

systemsmanager.q: How does Patch Manager keep servers up to date?
systemsmanager.a: It scans managed nodes for missing patches, or scans and installs them. Patch baselines say which patches are approved, and patch policies or maintenance windows set when patching runs.
systemsmanager.simple: Manny checks every server for missing fixes and installs the approved ones on a timetable.

systemsmanager.a: A document of steps that Systems Manager Automation carries out, such as restarting an instance or updating an AMI. AWS provides ready-made runbooks, you can write your own, and a run can need approval or span accounts and Regions.
systemsmanager.simple: A runbook is a written-down job that Manny carries out for you, the same way every time.

systemsmanager.a: It keeps managed nodes and other resources in a state you define, running Systems Manager documents on a schedule: install software at start-up, keep agents up to date or set network settings.
systemsmanager.simple: Manny keeps checking each server is set up the way you asked, on a regular round.

systemsmanager.q: What does Default Host Management Configuration do?
systemsmanager.a: It lets Systems Manager manage every EC2 instance in an account and Region automatically, through a default IAM role, so you don't attach an instance profile to each one. Instances then get Session Manager, Patch Manager and agent updates.
systemsmanager.simple: Flip one switch and Manny looks after every server in the account, with no setup for each one.

config.a: Cora's service records how your AWS resources are set up, how they relate to each other and how that changed over time. Rules then check those settings and flag resources that break them.
config.simple: Cora writes down how everything is set up and every change, then flags whatever breaks the rules.

config.a: A point-in-time record of one resource: its settings, metadata, relationships and related events. AWS Config creates one whenever a resource it records is created, changed or deleted.
config.simple: A snapshot of one thing's settings at one moment, taken each time it changes.

config.a: By configuration items recorded, rule evaluations and conformance pack evaluations. Continuous recording makes an item for every change; periodic recording makes at most one a day per resource. S3 and SNS charges apply too.
config.simple: You pay per change Cora records and per rule check. Recording once a day costs less for busy things.

config.q: What does the configuration recorder do?
config.a: It stores changes to the resource types in scope as configuration items. By default, a customer managed recorder records every supported resource type in the Region where AWS Config runs.
config.simple: The recorder is Cora's notebook. By default she writes down every kind of thing she can in the Region.

config.q: What do AWS Config rules do?
config.a: They describe the settings you want. AWS Config evaluates resources against each rule and marks them COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT. Managed rules are ready-made by AWS; custom rules run your own checks.
config.simple: A rule says how things should be. Cora marks each resource as following it or not.

config.q: When does an AWS Config rule run?
config.a: When a resource in its scope changes, on a schedule such as every 24 hours, or both. Proactive rules can also check settings before a resource is deployed, though they don't block it.
config.simple: Cora checks when something changes, on a timetable, or both. She can even check a plan before it is built.

config.q: How does AWS Config differ from CloudTrail?
config.a: CloudTrail records API calls: who did what, and when. AWS Config records what resources look like: their settings and how they changed. Together they show who changed a resource and what it looked like before and after.
config.simple: CloudTrail notes who did something. Config notes how things looked before and after.

config.a: A collection of AWS Config rules and remediation actions, written as a YAML template and deployed as one unit in an account and Region, or across an organization. AWS provides sample packs to start from.
config.simple: A ready-made set of rules Cora checks together, put in place in one go.

config.q: How can AWS Config fix a broken setting?
config.a: With remediation: you attach a Systems Manager Automation document to a rule, and it runs on noncompliant resources when you choose, or automatically. AWS provides managed remediation documents, and you can write your own.
config.simple: Cora calls on one of Manny's runbooks to put a broken setting right, by hand or automatically.

config.a: It collects AWS Config data from many accounts and Regions, or from a whole organization, into one account and Region. The view is read-only: you can't deploy rules through it.
config.simple: One office sees every account's records, though it can only look, not change anything.

config.q: What are advanced queries in AWS Config?
config.a: A subset of SQL SELECT that searches the current settings of your resources, without calling each service's own describe APIs. Through an aggregator, the same query runs across accounts and Regions.
config.simple: Ask Cora questions in SQL, like which servers are a certain type, across every account at once.

organizations.a: Orla's service for running many AWS accounts together. You create or invite accounts, group them, apply policies to them and pay for all of them with one bill.
organizations.simple: Orla groups all your AWS accounts, sets their rules and pays one bill for all of them.

organizations.q: What are the management account and member accounts?
organizations.a: The management account creates the organization, adds accounts, attaches policies and pays every account's charges. Every other account is a member account, and an account can belong to only one organization at a time.
organizations.simple: One account runs the council and pays the bills. The rest are members, each in one council only.

organizations.a: Nothing: AWS Organizations is offered at no additional charge. With consolidated billing, the management account gets a single bill covering the usage of every account.
organizations.simple: Organizations itself is free, and all your accounts share one bill.

organizations.a: A group of accounts inside the organization, such as all the production accounts or all the security accounts. OUs can hold other OUs, forming a tree under the root, and a policy attached to an OU applies to the accounts inside it.
organizations.simple: An OU is a ward of accounts. A rule set on the ward applies to every account in it.

organizations.q: What does a service control policy (SCP) do?
organizations.a: It sets the most that IAM users and roles in member accounts can do, such as using only certain Regions or services. An SCP never grants permissions: people still need IAM policies that allow the action.
organizations.simple: An SCP is a by-law that caps what anyone in an account may do. It never hands out extra rights.

organizations.q: Why keep workloads out of the management account?
organizations.a: SCPs don't restrict users or roles in the management account, so it can't be fenced in like the others. AWS recommends using it only for tasks that must run there and keeping resources in member accounts.
organizations.simple: The council's own account isn't bound by the by-laws, so keep the real work in member accounts.

organizations.q: What is a resource control policy (RCP)?
organizations.a: An organization policy that caps the permissions available on resources in member accounts, for example so only identities from your organization can reach them. SCPs limit your own people and roles; RCPs guard your resources.
organizations.simple: A resource rule guards the buildings themselves: no one from outside the town gets in.

organizations.a: A member account that the management account lets run an integrated AWS service, such as GuardDuty, for the whole organization, or manage organization policies. It keeps day-to-day work out of the management account.
organizations.simple: Orla hands one member account the keys to run a job for the whole town.

organizations.q: What is trusted access for an AWS service?
organizations.a: Turning it on lets a supported service, such as AWS Config or CloudFormation StackSets, work across the accounts in your organization. The service creates a service-linked role in an account when it needs one.
organizations.simple: Trusted access lets a service like Config do its job in every account in the town.

organizations.q: What are declarative policies, like tag and backup policies?
organizations.a: Organization policies that set up services across accounts: tag policies standardise tags, backup policies apply backup plans, and others set Amazon EC2 or Amazon S3 settings, so every account follows the same setup.
organizations.simple: Town-wide settings, like how to label things and when to back up, set once for every account.

organizations.q: Is AWS Organizations run per Region?
organizations.a: No. Its service endpoints are in US East (N. Virginia) for commercial organizations, and organization entities are global, like IAM, so you don't pick a Region. Accounts used in China need a separate organization.
organizations.simple: There is one council for every Region, run from North Virginia, a bit like IAM.

appsync.a: Gracie's service for serverless GraphQL and real-time APIs. One API endpoint can reach many data sources and push live updates to apps, and you pay for the requests and real-time messages.
appsync.simple: Gracie connects your app to all its data through one line, and calls back when something changes.

appsync.q: How is GraphQL different from a classic web API?
appsync.a: In a classic (REST) API each resource has its own address, so an app may make many calls and get back extra data. With GraphQL, the app asks one endpoint for exactly the fields it needs, from many sources, in one request.
appsync.simple: Instead of visiting many counters, you hand Gracie one list and get back exactly what's on it.

appsync.a: Per million query and data modification operations, per million real-time updates and per minute of connection. A server-side cache is billed by the hour. Requests that fail authorization aren't charged.
appsync.simple: You pay per request and per live update. Requests that fail the sign-in check are free.

appsync.q: What do queries, mutations and subscriptions do?
appsync.a: A query reads data, a mutation changes it, and a subscription keeps a connection open so the app hears about changes. In AppSync, subscriptions are triggered by mutations.
appsync.simple: A query asks, a mutation changes, and a subscription listens out for news.

appsync.a: The blueprint of the API, written in the Schema Definition Language: types with fields that describe the data and how it can be read or changed. It's the contract between the app and the server.
appsync.simple: The schema is the menu: every kind of data you can ask for, and its exact shape.

appsync.a: Code attached to a field in the schema that says how to read or change that field's data in a data source, such as DynamoDB, Lambda, OpenSearch, an HTTP endpoint or a relational database. Resolvers are written in JavaScript or VTL.
appsync.simple: A resolver is Gracie's note for each item on the menu: which place to ring to get it.

appsync.q: How does an AppSync API decide who may call it?
appsync.a: With five authorization types: API keys, AWS Lambda, IAM, OpenID Connect and Amazon Cognito user pools. You pick a default and can add more modes, for example Cognito for people and IAM for back-end services.
appsync.simple: Gracie checks each caller by an API key, a sign-in pass, IAM or your own Lambda check.

appsync.q: How do subscriptions deliver live updates?
appsync.a: When an app subscribes, AppSync opens and keeps up a secure WebSocket connection. Matching changes are pushed to subscribers in real time, and AppSync handles the connections and the scaling.
appsync.simple: Gracie keeps a line open to each phone and rings it the moment something changes.

appsync.a: A resolver that runs a list of functions in order, between a Before and an After step, each against its own data source: for example, check a user's permission, then save the item.
appsync.simple: Gracie rings several places in turn for one request, like checking a pass, then saving the order.

appsync.a: Server-side caching keeps resolver results in a dedicated in-memory cache (ElastiCache) that AppSync runs for you, so repeat requests skip the data source and answer faster. The cache is billed per hour by size.
appsync.simple: Gracie keeps popular answers on a notepad, so she doesn't ring the same place twice.

appsync.a: They let teams build and deploy their own AppSync source APIs on their own, then combine them into one merged GraphQL API. Apps get a single endpoint while each team ships at its own pace.
appsync.simple: Each team runs its own switchboard, and Gracie joins them into one number for callers.

appsync.a: Serverless WebSocket APIs for publishing and subscribing: broadcast real-time events to millions of subscribers, with no API code needed to start and no connections to manage.
appsync.simple: A loudspeaker for live news: send one message and millions of listening apps hear it.

appsync.q: What is an AppSync Private API?
appsync.a: An API that can only be reached from your VPC, through interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). Apps inside need no public IP addresses, and traffic doesn't leave the AWS network.
appsync.simple: A private line that only callers inside your own network can use.
